begriffe.erklaerung: A castle surrounded by water, which made it better protected.
An official who governed an area on behalf of a town or a lord.
A fee you have to pay for goods at a border or on a road.
Careful repair of an old building so that it looks as it used to.

gewusst: Lord Byron carved his name into a pillar in the dungeon, and you can still see it today.
The castle has about 100 building sections, rooms and courtyards that have grown together over the centuries.
The rock on which Chillon stands drops very steeply into the lake, so the water right next to it is deep.

teile.einleitung: A state is an area with borders in which a people lives and a government sets the rules. Switzerland, France, Japan and Australia are examples of states. There are just under 200 states on Earth, each with its own capital, language and culture.
wichtigste: A state has a territory, a people and state authority.
193 states belong to the United Nations; Switzerland has been a member since 2002.
Every state has a capital: Paris, for example, is in France and Tokyo in Japan.
In Switzerland the Federal Council and parliament work in Bern.
Switzerland's neighbours are Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.
In Italy people speak Italian; Switzerland has four national languages.
The largest state is Russia, the smallest is Vatican City.

abschnitte.text: According to a well-known theory, a state needs three things. It has a **territory** with borders, a **people**, that is the people who live there, and **state authority** that makes laws and enforces them. The state provides, for example, schools, roads, police and courts. People pay taxes for this.

There are just under 200 states on Earth, and 193 of them are members of the United Nations. Each has a **capital**, for example Paris in France, Rome in Italy or Tokyo in Japan. States differ in size, language, climate and nature. In Australia, for example, kangaroos live in the wild, and nowhere else in the world.

Switzerland is a **federal state** made up of 26 cantons, which decide many things for themselves. The Federal Council and parliament work in the Federal Palace in Bern. Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. Its neighbouring countries are Germany, France, Italy, Austria and Liechtenstein.

There are different **forms of state**. In a republic the head of state is elected, as in France or Italy. In a monarchy there is a king, a queen or a prince, as in Great Britain or Liechtenstein. In a democracy the citizens have a say, and in Switzerland they even vote very often.

By area the largest state in the world is **Russia**: it is more than 400 times the size of Switzerland. India and China have the most inhabitants, each with more than 1.4 billion people. The smallest state is **Vatican City**, in the middle of Rome. Liechtenstein, our neighbour, is also one of the smallest states in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: The land within the borders of a state.
The city where the government and parliament of a country are usually based.
A state without a king, in which the head of state is elected for a limited time.
A state with a king, a queen or a prince at its head.
A state made up of several member states; in Switzerland these are the cantons.

gewusst: Vatican City is so small that you can walk round it in about half an hour.
Switzerland only joined the United Nations in 2002, after a popular vote.
The constitution does not say capital: Bern is officially called the federal city.

teile.einleitung: A weighing puzzle is a brain teaser in which you have to find something out as cleverly as possible using a balance scale. A well-known example: among 9 coins that look the same, one is heavier. If you go about it cleverly, you can find it with only 2 weighings.
wichtigste: In weighing puzzles you use a balance scale without a weight display.
A balance scale has three possible results: left heavier, right heavier or equal.
Among 9 coins you can find the heavier one with 2 weighings.
The trick is to divide the coins into three groups of equal size.
With 3 weighings you can even find the heavier coin among 27 coins in this way.
The puzzle is harder if you do not know whether the fake coin is lighter or heavier.

abschnitte.text: A **balance scale** has two pans on a beam. It does not show a number, only which side is heavier or whether both are equal. In a weighing puzzle you are supposed to uncover a secret with as few weighings as possible. Usually it is about finding one fake item among many identical ones.

You divide the 9 coins into three groups of 3 coins each. You put two of the groups on the scale. If one side is heavier, the coin you are looking for is there; if both are equal, it is in the third group. For the **second weighing** you take two of the 3 suspect coins and compare them. In this way you always find the heavy coin with exactly 2 weighings.

Because the scale can have **three results**, each weighing rules out two thirds of the possibilities. With one weighing you can find the heavy coin among 3, with two among 9, with three among 27 coins. Mathematically these are the **powers** of 3. If you only divide the coins into two groups, you waste the third possibility and need more weighings.

It gets even trickier with 12 coins, one of which is fake. But you do not know whether it is **lighter or heavier**. Even so, you can find it with 3 weighings and at the same time find out whether it is too light or too heavy. This puzzle has been popular with puzzle fans for many decades.

Weighing puzzles train **logical thinking** and planning. You learn to break a task down into steps and rule out possibilities. Similar ideas are needed in computer science, when a computer has to search for something quickly in a large set. Puzzles like these also appear in school competitions such as the Mathematical Kangaroo.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scale with two pans that shows which side is heavier.
One single time when you put something on the scale and compare.
A number multiplied by itself several times, for example 3 times 3 equals 9.
The art of thinking correctly and step by step.

gewusst: With just 4 weighings you could even find the heavier coin among 81 coins.
With the four weights 1, 3, 9 and 27 kilograms you can weigh any whole weight from 1 to 40 kilograms, if you are allowed to put weights on both pans.
The balance scale is a symbol of justice and is often shown with the figure of Lady Justice.

teile.einleitung: A riddle is a tricky question or task where you have to think outside the box to find the answer. Riddles have existed for thousands of years in all the cultures of the world. They are fun, train the brain and often make everyone laugh when the answer is finally clear.
wichtigste: A riddle hides the answer behind a clever description.
Many riddles play with words that have several meanings.
Well-known kinds are joke questions, picture puzzles, crosswords and logic puzzles.
Riddles already play an important part in old legends such as the one about the Sphinx.
The first crossword appeared in a New York newspaper in 1913.
Solving riddles trains careful reading, patience and creative thinking.
Often the answer is very simple: you just have to take the question literally.

abschnitte.text: In a **riddle**, something is described in such a way that you do not recognise it straight away. You have to think, put things together and sometimes think quite differently from usual. Often the description seems impossible at first, until you discover the trick. One example is: what gets wet while it dries? The answer is: a towel, because it dries other things and gets wet itself in the process.

Many riddles use words with **several meanings**. A comb has teeth but cannot bite. A river has a bed but never sleeps, because the riverbed is the ground it flows over. A table has four legs but cannot walk. Riddles like these are often called **joke questions**, because they play with what we expect.

Some riddles set a trap that you easily fall into. Which is heavier, a kilo of feathers or a kilo of stones? Both are equally heavy, because a kilo is a kilo. Which month has 28 days? All of them, because every month has at least 28 days. And if Anna's mother has three children, Lena, Tim and one more, then the third child is of course **Anna** herself.

Riddles are ancient and appear in many legends and fairy tales. In the Greek legend, the **Sphinx** outside the city of Thebes asked every traveller a riddle: what walks on four legs in the morning, on two at midday and on three in the evening? The hero Oedipus found the answer: a human being, who crawls as a baby, walks as an adult and needs a stick in old age. In the fairy tale of Rumpelstiltskin, too, the queen has to solve a riddle, namely guess a name. On 21 December 1913 the first **crossword** appeared in the newspaper ‘New York World’.

Today there are many different kinds of riddles. In a **picture puzzle**, also called a rebus, you have to make a word out of pictures and letters. In sudoku you fill in a grid of numbers so that every digit from 1 to 9 appears exactly once in each row, column and box. Logic puzzles ask you to work out the answer step by step from clues. The Rubik's Cube, escape rooms and many computer games are also a kind of riddle.

begriffe.erklaerung: A funny riddle with a surprising answer, often a play on words.
A picture puzzle in which pictures and letters together make a word.
When a word or sentence can have two different meanings.
The art of thinking correctly and consistently.

gewusst: The Rubik's Cube was invented in 1974 by the Hungarian architect Ernő Rubik and is one of the best-selling toys in the world.
Although the name sounds Japanese, sudoku goes back to a number puzzle that was first published in the USA.
Solving riddles can train the memory, which is why they are also very popular with older people.

teile.einleitung: Compound interest is the interest you get on interest you have already received. If the interest stays in the account, the money grows a little faster every year. Given enough time, a small amount can turn into a large sum.
wichtigste: Interest is the price you pay for borrowed money or receive for money you have saved.
With compound interest, the interest is added to the capital and earns interest itself the next year.
10,000 francs at 2 % interest a year become 10,612.08 francs after 3 years with compound interest.
The longer you save, the stronger the effect of compound interest.
The formula is: final capital equals starting capital times (1 plus interest rate) to the power of the number of years.
Compound interest also works on debts, for example on credit cards, and makes them grow quickly.
The rule of thumb 72 divided by the interest rate shows roughly after how many years an amount doubles.

abschnitte.text: If you put money into a **savings account**, you are lending it to the bank. In return the bank pays **interest**, for example 2 % a year. If you leave this interest in the account, it becomes part of the capital the next year. Then you get interest on the money and on the old interest. That is exactly what is called **compound interest**.

Let us take 10,000 francs at 2 % interest a year. After one year there are 10,200 francs, because 2 % of 10,000 is 200 francs. In the second year you get 2 % of 10,200, that is 204 francs, and you have 10,404 francs. In the third year 208.08 francs are added. So after 3 years there are exactly **10,612.08 francs** in the account, 12.08 francs more than with simple interest.

You do not have to calculate each year separately. There is the **compound interest formula**: final capital equals starting capital times (1 plus p/100) to the power of n. Here p is the interest rate in per cent and n is the number of years. For our example this means 10,000 times 1.02 to the power of 3. Because the curve gets steeper and steeper, this is called **exponential growth**.

With compound interest, time matters most of all. Someone who starts saving at 20 often ends up with much more than someone who only starts at 40, even if both pay in the same amount. With the **rule of 72** you can estimate how long it takes to double: at 2 % interest it takes about 36 years, at 6 % only about 12 years. That is why people are often advised to start saving early.

Unfortunately, compound interest also works the other way round. If you have debts and do not pay the interest, you will soon have to pay interest on the interest too. **Credit cards** and **consumer loans** are especially expensive; in Switzerland they can have interest rates of up to about 10 to 12 % a year. In this way a small debt can quickly become large. That is why it is wise to pay back debts as quickly as possible.

In Switzerland there are youth savings accounts, which often offer slightly higher interest. The **pension fund** and pillar 3a also use compound interest over many decades. How high interest rates are depends greatly on the Swiss National Bank's policy rate. In some years there was almost no interest at all, in others considerably more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The money that you have invested or borrowed.
How many per cent interest there is per year.
Something grows faster and faster, because each time it increases by a share of what has already grown.
How much profit an investment brings in per year.

gewusst: If you invested a single franc for 500 years at 5 % compound interest, you would end up with almost 40 billion francs.
As long ago as ancient Babylon, more than 4000 years ago, people calculated interest on interest.
With simple interest, money grows like a staircase with steps of equal height; with compound interest the steps get higher and higher.

teile.einleitung: Venus is the second planet from the sun and our nearest neighbour in the solar system. It is almost the same size as the Earth, but the heat there is unimaginable. And it has a special feature: a day on Venus lasts longer than a whole Venus year.
wichtigste: Venus is the second planet from the sun.
It is roughly the same size as the Earth.
At about 460 degrees Celsius on its surface, it is the hottest planet.
One rotation on its own axis takes 243 Earth days, but one orbit round the sun only 225 days.
Venus spins in the opposite direction to most planets.
After the sun and the moon, it is the brightest object in the night sky.
Venus has no moon.

abschnitte.text: Venus has a diameter of about 12,100 kilometres, which makes it only slightly smaller than the Earth. On average it is about 108 million kilometres from the sun. Like the Earth it is a **rocky planet** with a solid surface. That is why it is sometimes called the Earth's sister.

abschnitte.titel: The hell of the solar system
abschnitte.text: The **atmosphere** of Venus consists mostly of carbon dioxide. This gas traps the heat like the panes of a greenhouse. That is why, at about 460 degrees, it is hotter there than on Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the sun. The air pressure is about 90 times as high as on Earth. Thick clouds of **sulphuric acid** cover the whole planet.

Venus takes 225 Earth days to go round the sun once. But it takes 243 Earth days to turn once on its own axis. So a day is longer than a year. In addition it rotates **backwards**, that is the other way round from the Earth. That is why on Venus the sun would rise in the west and set in the east.

Because its clouds reflect sunlight strongly, Venus shines very brightly. You can see it either in the morning before sunrise or in the evening after sunset. That is why it is also called the **morning star** or the **evening star**, even though it is not a star at all. It is named after the Roman goddess of love.

The Soviet Union sent several space probes called **Venera** to Venus. In 1970 Venera 7 became the first probe to land on another planet and radio data back to Earth. Because of the heat and pressure, the landers only lasted a short time. In the early 1990s the American probe Magellan mapped the surface with radar. It revealed thousands of volcanoes and wide plains of lava.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large body in space that circles a star such as the sun.
The layer of gases surrounding a planet.
Gases trap the heat, so that a planet heats up a lot.
An uncrewed spacecraft that explores other bodies in space.

gewusst: It is so hot on Venus that lead would melt.
Venus is the only planet in our solar system named after a female deity.
Sometimes bright Venus in the sky is mistaken for an aeroplane or even a UFO.

teile.einleitung: The Industrial Revolution was a time of great change in which machines and factories increasingly replaced work done by hand. It began in Great Britain in the 18th century and then spread across Europe and the world. It decisively shaped our life today, with electricity, railways and mass-produced goods.
wichtigste: The Industrial Revolution began around 1760 in Great Britain.
Great Britain had rich deposits of coal and iron and plenty of capital from trade.
The steam engine, improved by James Watt, became the most important source of power.
In factories, machines made cloth and other goods much faster than by hand.
From the 19th century, railways connected cities and countries.
Many people moved from the countryside to the towns to work in factories.
Switzerland was one of the first countries on the European mainland to industrialise.

abschnitte.text: Before the **Industrial Revolution**, most people lived from farming and made goods by hand. Then machines were invented that could produce much more and much faster. Instead of working in small workshops, people now worked in large **factories**. This upheaval changed work, housing and the whole way people lived together.

In the 18th century Great Britain had especially good conditions. There were rich supplies of **coal** and iron ore, and thanks to trade and colonies there was plenty of money to invest in new factories. On top of that there were good ports, canals and a large market for goods. Many inventors and entrepreneurs looked for ways to produce faster and more cheaply.

In textile making, spinning machines such as the spinning jenny sped up the work enormously from the 1760s. From 1769 **James Watt** improved the **steam engine**, which now powered factories, mines and later ships. In 1825 the first public railway with a steam locomotive ran in England between Stockton and Darlington. New processes made iron and later steel cheaper and available in large quantities.

Work in the factories was hard, often 12 to 14 hours a day and six days a week. Children had to work too, often from the age of six or seven. In the fast-growing towns, many families lived in cramped, dirty homes. Workers joined together in **trade unions** and fought for shorter working hours, better wages and protective laws.

Switzerland's first mechanical spinning mill started operating in Winterthur-Wülflingen in 1801. Soon textile factories sprang up in the Zurich Oberland, the Glarus region and eastern Switzerland, powered by the **water power** of the rivers. In 1847 the Spanisch-Brötli-Bahn between Zurich and Baden became Switzerland's first railway. The federal **Factory Act** of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14 and limited the working day to eleven hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: The making of goods in large quantities with machines.
A machine that uses hot steam to produce movement.
A large business in which many people make goods with machines.
An association of employees that stands up for their rights.
Money or property that you use to build up a business.

gewusst: In 1832 home weavers in Uster, afraid of losing their work, set fire to a mechanical weaving mill; this event is called the Usterbrand (Uster fire).
Because Swiss factories were at first driven by water wheels, they were built mainly along rivers rather than in large cities.
The unit watt, used today to measure the power of light bulbs and appliances, is named after James Watt.

teile.einleitung: The European Free Trade Association, EFTA for short, is a group of European states that want to trade freely with each other. Today EFTA is made up of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Unlike the EU, it is not a political union but mainly a trading community.
wichtigste: EFTA was founded in 1960.
It has four members: Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein (as of 2026).
Switzerland is one of the founding members.
The EFTA Secretariat is based in Geneva.
There are no customs duties between the members on most industrial goods.
EFTA makes joint free trade agreements with countries all over the world.
Unlike the other three members, Switzerland is not in the European Economic Area.

abschnitte.text: EFTA is the abbreviation of the English name European Free Trade Association. Its members charge each other no **customs duties** on most industrial goods. So goods do not become more expensive when they cross the border, and trade becomes simpler. Unlike in the EU, there is no shared parliament and no shared currency.

EFTA was founded in 1960 with the Treaty of **Stockholm**. The founding members were Switzerland, Austria, Denmark, Norway, Portugal, Sweden and Great Britain. These countries wanted to trade freely with each other but not to join the European Economic Community of the time. Later Iceland, Finland and Liechtenstein joined.

Over time many members left EFTA to join the **European Union** and its forerunners. Great Britain and Denmark switched in 1973, Portugal in 1986 and Austria, Sweden and Finland in 1995. Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein were left. Liechtenstein has been a full member since 1991.

Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are closely linked to the EU single market through the **European Economic Area**. Swiss voters narrowly rejected joining the EEA on 6 December 1992. Since then Switzerland has governed its relationship with the EU through **bilateral agreements**. EFTA remains important for Switzerland because, together with its partners, it makes free trade agreements worldwide.

The EFTA states have together made many free trade agreements with countries outside Europe. These include, for example, Canada, Mexico, South Korea and India. Agreements like these help Swiss companies export watches, machines, medicines or cheese more cheaply. The Secretariat in **Geneva** handles the negotiations and administration.

begriffe.erklaerung: Trade between countries without customs duties and other obstacles.
A charge you have to pay when you bring goods across a border.
European Economic Area, which links the EU with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.
Agreements between two partners, for example between Switzerland and the EU.

gewusst: EFTA has fewer members today than when it was founded.
With about 40,000 inhabitants, Liechtenstein is the smallest member of EFTA.
The agreement between EFTA and India provides for the EFTA countries to invest there on a large scale.

teile.einleitung: Wangari Maathai was an environmentalist from Kenya who, together with the women working with her, planted millions of trees. In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. She showed that protecting the environment, women's rights and peace belong together.
wichtigste: Wangari Maathai lived from 1940 to 2011 and came from Kenya.
She was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate.
In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement.
The movement planted several dozen million trees in Africa.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
She also fought for democracy and women's rights.
Later she was a member of parliament and assistant minister for the environment in Kenya.

abschnitte.text: Wangari Maathai was born on 1 April 1940 in a village in central **Kenya**. She belonged to the Kikuyu people and grew up in the countryside. As a good pupil she got a scholarship and studied biology in the USA. Later, in Nairobi, she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a **doctorate**. She became a professor at the University of Nairobi.

In 1977 she founded the **Green Belt Movement**. She saw that many forests were being cut down and the soil was drying out. Because of this, women had to walk further and further to find firewood and water. Maathai paid women to grow and plant tree seedlings. In this way several dozen million new trees were planted, and many women earned their own money.

Maathai took on the Kenyan government of the time. In 1989 she protested against a huge tower block that was to be built in **Uhuru Park** in Nairobi, and she succeeded. She also campaigned to protect Karura Forest. Because of her work she was arrested several times and was even injured. Even so, she never gave up.

In 2004 she received the **Nobel Peace Prize** for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace. She was the first African woman to receive this prize. The Nobel Committee stressed that quarrels over scarce water and land often lead to wars. So anyone who protects the environment also protects peace.

From 2002 Maathai was a member of parliament and then assistant minister for the environment. She wrote several books, including the story of her life. She died of cancer in Nairobi on 25 September 2011. Her movement is still working today and has inspired people all over the world to **plant trees**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A woman who works publicly and through her actions to protect nature.
A very famous prize for people who work especially hard for peace.
Cutting down so many trees that forests disappear.
Acting in a way that allows future generations to live well too.

gewusst: Maathai liked to tell the story of a little hummingbird that carries drops of water to a forest fire and says: I am doing what I can.
Her movement paid a small sum for every seedling that survived.
She was 64 years old when she received the Nobel Peace Prize.

teile.einleitung: Novak Djokovic is a tennis player from Serbia and one of the most successful athletes of all time. He holds the record for the most Grand Slam titles in men's singles. With his agility, his strong return of serve and his fighting spirit, he has won almost everything there is to win in tennis.
wichtigste: Novak Djokovic was born on 22 May 1987 in Belgrade in Serbia.
He holds the record with 24 Grand Slam titles in men's singles.
He won the Australian Open alone ten times, more often than any other man.
He was world number 1 for longer than any other player.
In 2024 he won the Olympic gold medal in Paris.
With Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal he formed tennis's ‘Big Three’.
He celebrated his 100th tournament win in Geneva in 2025.

abschnitte.text: Novak Djokovic was born in **Belgrade** on 22 May 1987. His parents ran a pizzeria in the Kopaonik ski resort, where he was already playing tennis at the age of four. The coach **Jelena Genčić** discovered his talent and trained him intensively. His childhood was not easy, because in 1999 Belgrade was bombed during the Kosovo War. At 12 he went to a tennis academy in Munich so that he could train better.

The **Grand Slam tournaments** are the four most important tennis tournaments: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open. Djokovic won his first Grand Slam title in Melbourne in 2008. By 2023 he had reached a total of 24 titles, more than any other man. Of these, he won 10 in Australia, 7 at Wimbledon, 4 at the US Open and 3 in Paris. This put him ahead of his great rivals Rafael Nadal with 22 and Roger Federer with 20 titles.

Djokovic was at the top of the **world rankings** for more than 400 weeks, a record. He won the ATP Finals, the tournament of the year's best eight players, seven times. In 2024 in Paris he fulfilled a big dream and won **Olympic gold** in the singles. In May 2025 he won his 100th title on the ATP Tour at the tournament in Geneva. He is one of only a few players to have won all four Grand Slam tournaments several times.

Djokovic is famous for his **agility**: he can slide almost into the splits on court. His return of serve, the **return**, is considered one of the best in history. He stays calm even in difficult moments and often turns round matches that seem already lost. For his fitness he pays great attention to his diet and, for example, eats no gluten. Many experts consider him the most complete player of all time.

For many years Djokovic, Federer and Nadal played most of the big finals among themselves. That is why they were called the **Big Three**. Djokovic has a winning record in head-to-head matches against both rivals. Later, younger players such as Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner challenged him. Through his foundation Djokovic supports nursery schools and education for children in Serbia.

begriffe.erklaerung: The four most important tennis tournaments in the world: in Melbourne, Paris, London and New York.
A list showing who is currently the best tennis player in the world.
The shot with which a player hits back the opponent's serve.
The nickname for the three exceptional players Federer, Nadal and Djokovic.

gewusst: Djokovic speaks several languages, including Serbian, English, German, Italian and French.
Of all places, he achieved his 100th tournament win in Switzerland, at the Geneva tournament in 2025.
In his first years as a professional, Djokovic often became known for his funny impressions of other players.

teile.einleitung: The Eiffel Tower is the most famous landmark of Paris and one of the best-known structures in the world. It was built in 1889 for the World’s Fair, which was held for the 100th anniversary of the French Revolution. At around 330 metres, it was for a long time the tallest structure on Earth.
wichtigste: The Eiffel Tower stands in Paris on the bank of the Seine.
It was built for the World’s Fair of 1889.
It is named after Gustave Eiffel, whose company built it.
With its antennas it is now about 330 metres tall.
Until 1930 it was the tallest structure in the world.
It is made of wrought iron and was built in just over two years.
About six million people visit it every year.

abschnitte.text: The Eiffel Tower is a lattice tower made of **wrought iron**. It consists of around 18,000 individual parts joined with about 2.5 million rivets. The iron structure alone weighs about 7300 tonnes. Thanks to the open design, the wind can blow through it easily.

In 1889 Paris held a great **World’s Fair** to celebrate 100 years since the French Revolution. As an entrance gate and attraction, the city wanted to build a tower taller than anything before. The plans came from the engineers Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier of **Gustave Eiffel**’s company. It was built from 1887 to 1889, so in just over two years.

Many artists and writers thought the tower was ugly and protested against it in newspapers. It was originally meant to be torn down again after 20 years. It was saved because it was needed for **radio antennas** and scientific measurements. Today it is the symbol of Paris and of all France.

When it opened, the tower was 312 metres tall, making it the tallest structure in the world. It lost this record only in 1930, to the Chrysler Building in New York. With new antennas it is now about 330 metres tall. To stop it rusting, it is repainted about every seven years, which takes around 60 tonnes of paint.

Visitors can reach three levels, either on foot or by lift. From the top platform, at a height of around 276 metres, you can see far across Paris in clear weather. In the tower there are restaurants and a small office that Gustave Eiffel once used. In the evening the tower sparkles for a few minutes every hour on the hour with thousands of **light bulbs**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A well-known structure by which you recognise a city at once.
A large exhibition at which countries show their inventions and achievements.
A metal pin used to join sheets and beams firmly together.
A tough iron that is easy to shape and work.

gewusst: In summer the iron expands in the heat, so the tower grows by a few centimetres.
Gustave Eiffel also built the inner framework of the Statue of Liberty in New York.
There are over 1600 steps up to the third level altogether, but the public may only walk as far as the second level.

teile.einleitung: The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of the planet Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. Galileo Galilei discovered them in January 1610 with a telescope he had built himself. They were the first moons ever found orbiting a planet other than Earth.
wichtigste: The four Galilean moons are called Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Galileo Galilei discovered them in 1610 with a telescope.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the whole solar system, even bigger than the planet Mercury.
Io has hundreds of active volcanoes.
Under Europa’s shell of ice, researchers suspect there is an ocean of water.
Callisto is covered with countless craters.
With good binoculars you can see the moons next to Jupiter as small points of light.

abschnitte.text: In January 1610 **Galileo Galilei** in Padua pointed his telescope at Jupiter. He saw three, later four, small points of light that changed their position from night to night. Galileo realised that they were circling Jupiter. He described the discovery in 1610 in his work “Sidereus Nuncius”, which means Starry Messenger.

abschnitte.titel: A new view of the world
abschnitte.text: At that time many people believed that everything revolved around the Earth. Jupiter’s moons showed that there are heavenly bodies that do not circle the Earth. This supported the **heliocentric view of the world** of Nicolaus Copernicus, in which the Sun is at the centre. Because of this, Galileo later came into conflict with the Catholic Church.

**Io** is the innermost of the four moons and the most volcanically active body in the solar system. Jupiter’s strong gravity constantly kneads Io and so heats it up. **Europa** is a little smaller than our Moon and is covered with a smooth layer of ice. Beneath it there is probably a salty ocean in which there might even be life.

**Ganymede** has a diameter of over 5000 kilometres, making it the largest moon in the solar system. It is the only known moon with its own magnetic field. **Callisto** is almost as big as the planet Mercury. Its dark surface is one of the most heavily cratered landscapes in the solar system.

The space probe Galileo explored the Jupiter system from 1995 to 2003. In 2023 the European probe **JUICE**, in which Switzerland is also involved, was launched; from 2031 it is to study mainly Ganymede. In 2024 NASA sent off the probe Europa Clipper, which is to explore the icy moon Europa. Today almost 100 moons of Jupiter are known, but the four Galilean ones are by far the largest.

begriffe.erklaerung: A heavenly body that circles a planet.
A device with lenses that makes distant things look bigger.
A view of the world in which the Sun is at the centre and the planets circle it.
An uncrewed spacecraft that explores other heavenly bodies.

gewusst: The German astronomer Simon Marius saw the moons at almost the same time as Galileo, and their present-day names come from him.
Galileo first called the moons the “Medicean Stars”, in honour of the powerful Medici family in Florence.
Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury but has only about half as much mass.

teile.einleitung: Marie Curie was a Polish-French physicist and chemist who lived from 1867 to 1934. She studied radioactivity and discovered the chemical elements polonium and radium. She was the first person to receive two Nobel Prizes, and in two different sciences.
wichtigste: Marie Curie was born Maria Skłodowska in Warsaw in 1867.
She studied at the Sorbonne in Paris.
With her husband Pierre Curie she studied radioactivity.
In 1898 she discovered the elements polonium and radium.
In 1903 she received the Nobel Prize in Physics, and in 1911 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
She is the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
She died in 1934 as a result of radiation.

abschnitte.text: Marie Curie was born in **Warsaw** on 7 November 1867; her name was Maria Skłodowska. At that time Poland belonged to the Russian Empire, and women were not allowed to go to university there. So Maria worked as a governess and saved money. In 1891 she moved to **Paris** to study physics and mathematics at the Sorbonne.

In Paris she met the physicist **Pierre Curie** and married him in 1895. She studied the mysterious rays given off by uranium and invented the word **radioactivity** for them. In 1898 the two of them discovered two new elements. She named one polonium after her homeland Poland, and the other radium, after the Latin word for ray.

In 1903 she received the **Nobel Prize in Physics** together with Pierre Curie and Henri Becquerel. She was the first woman ever to receive a Nobel Prize. In 1911 she received the **Nobel Prize in Chemistry** on her own for discovering polonium and radium. This made her the first person with two Nobel Prizes.

In 1906 Pierre Curie died in an accident with a horse-drawn cart. Marie took over his professorship and became the first female professor at the Sorbonne. In the First World War she equipped cars with **X-ray machines** to examine wounded soldiers. Her daughter Irène Joliot-Curie also received a Nobel Prize in Chemistry, in 1935.

At that time people did not yet know how dangerous radioactive radiation is. Marie Curie worked without protection and even carried samples in the pocket of her lab coat. She died on 4 July 1934 of a blood disease that was probably caused by the **radiation**. In 1995 she became the first woman to be buried in the **Panthéon** in Paris for her own achievements.

begriffe.erklaerung: Some substances give off invisible, high-energy rays all by themselves.
A basic substance from which all things are made, for example iron or oxygen.
A famous award for great achievements in science, literature and peace.
A device that lets you see inside the body, for example at the bones.

gewusst: Marie Curie's notebooks are still radioactive today and are kept in lead boxes.
The chemical element curium is named after Marie and Pierre Curie.
The Curie family has won five Nobel Prizes in total.

teile.einleitung: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge in China is the longest bridge in the world. It is a railway viaduct around 165 kilometres long that carries high-speed trains. That is roughly as far as from Zurich to Bern and a good bit further.
wichtigste: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge is in China and, at around 165 kilometres, is the longest bridge in the world (as of 2026).
It is a viaduct for the high-speed line between Beijing and Shanghai.
The bridge opened in 2011.
It lies in Jiangsu province in eastern China.
A section about 9 kilometres long runs over water.
The bridge is in the Guinness Book of Records.

abschnitte.text: The bridge lies in **Jiangsu** province in eastern China, not far from Shanghai. It connects the cities of Danyang and Kunshan, passing Nanjing, Wuxi and Suzhou on the way. The area is very flat and full of rivers, canals, lakes and rice fields. Part of the route crosses Yangcheng Lake.

The bridge is part of the Beijing-Shanghai **high-speed line**, which opened in 2011. High-speed trains travel on it at over 300 kilometres per hour. The whole line between the two cities of millions is over 1300 kilometres long. By train this journey now takes only around four and a half to six hours.

On soft ground, in wet areas and over water, a **viaduct** is often better than an earth embankment. The piers stand firmly in the ground, and the land underneath stays free. So ships, cars, farmers and animals can pass under the railway without obstruction. It also saves valuable farmland.

The bridge was built in about four years, from 2006 to 2010. Around 10,000 workers took part. The bridge consists of many identical concrete sections lying on thousands of **piers**. This way of building with prefabricated parts made the huge project possible more quickly.

According to the **Guinness Book of Records**, the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge is the longest bridge in the world. The next places are taken by other railway bridges in China. By comparison, the longest bridge in Switzerland is only a few kilometres long. If you laid the Chinese bridge across Switzerland, it would reach almost from Geneva to Bern.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long bridge on many piers that crosses a valley or flat land.
A strong column on which a bridge rests.
An especially fast train that travels at over 250 kilometres per hour.
A large part of a country in China, similar to a canton in Switzerland.

gewusst: A high-speed train needs only about half an hour to cross the whole bridge.
Almost all the longest bridges in the world are railway viaducts in China.
From above, the bridge looks like an endless grey ribbon running through fields and villages.

teile.einleitung: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648, one of the worst wars in European history. It was negotiated in the towns of Münster and Osnabrück in Westphalia. For Switzerland it was especially important: the Swiss Confederation was recognised as independent of the Holy Roman Empire.
wichtigste: The Peace of Westphalia was concluded in 1648.
It ended the Thirty Years' War, which had begun in 1618.
Negotiations took place in Münster and Osnabrück.
The separation of the Swiss Confederation from the Holy Roman Empire was recognised.
The mayor of Basel, Johann Rudolf Wettstein, represented the Swiss.
The Netherlands were also recognised as independent.
The treaty is seen as the beginning of the modern order of equal states.

abschnitte.text: From 1618 to 1648 the **Thirty Years' War** raged in Central Europe. It began as a dispute between Catholic and Protestant princes. Soon Sweden, France and Spain also got involved. Many areas of today's Germany were devastated, and in many places a large part of the population died from fighting, hunger and epidemics.

From the 1640s envoys from all over Europe met in **Münster** and **Osnabrück**. It was one of the first great peace congresses in history. The negotiations lasted several years, while fighting continued elsewhere. On 24 October 1648 the peace treaties were signed.

Formally, the Swiss Confederation still belonged to the **Holy Roman Empire**, but since the Swabian War of 1499 it had been practically independent. The mayor of Basel, **Johann Rudolf Wettstein**, travelled to Westphalia. He achieved the Confederation's official release from the rule of the Empire. Since then Switzerland's independence has also been recognised under international law.

Catholics, Lutherans and the **Reformed** were recognised as having equal rights in the Empire. The Netherlands finally became independent of Spain. France and Sweden gained new territories. The individual princes in the Empire got more rights and could, for example, form alliances themselves.

The Peace of Westphalia is regarded as the foundation stone of modern **international law**. The idea was that states are equal and independent and settle their disputes at the negotiating table. That is why people speak of the Westphalian system. You can still visit the halls in Münster and Osnabrück where the negotiations took place.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without war, often laid down in a treaty.
A representative sent by a country or ruler to negotiations.
Rules that apply between states.
A large empire in Central Europe that existed from the Middle Ages until 1806 and was ruled by an emperor.

gewusst: That is why Münster and Osnabrück call themselves cities of peace today.
Wettstein was originally not sent by all the cantons of the Confederation, but mainly by Basel and the Reformed cantons.
The negotiations in Westphalia were conducted mainly in Latin and French.

teile.einleitung: In geometry, a diagonal is a straight line that joins two corners of a polygon that are not next to each other. A square has two diagonals, which cross in the middle. The more corners a shape has, the faster the number of its diagonals grows.
wichtigste: A diagonal joins two corners of a polygon that are not neighbours.
A triangle has no diagonals.
A quadrilateral has two diagonals, a pentagon five.
A convex decagon has 35 diagonals.
The number is calculated with the formula n times (n minus 3) divided by 2.
In a square, both diagonals are the same length and are at right angles to each other.
Screen sizes are given by the diagonal.

abschnitte.text: The word **diagonal** comes from Greek and means roughly “through the angles”. A diagonal runs across a shape from one corner to another. The edges of the shape, the sides, do not count as diagonals. In everyday life too, people say diagonal when something runs at a slant.

From each corner of a polygon with n corners, n minus 3 diagonals go out. After all, you do not draw one to the corner itself or to its two neighbours. Because each diagonal has two ends, you calculate **n times (n minus 3) divided by 2**. For a decagon this gives 10 times 7 divided by 2, which is 35 diagonals.

In a square the two diagonals are the same length, cut each other in half and are at right angles to each other. In a **rectangle** they are also the same length, but usually do not cross at right angles. In a **rhombus** they are at right angles but have different lengths. The diagonal of a square with side length 1 is about 1.41 long, which is the square root of 2.

If you draw all five diagonals in a regular pentagon, you get a five-pointed star. This star is called a **pentagram**. The ancient Greeks already studied this figure. Inside the star a small pentagon forms again.

The size of televisions, mobile phones and computer screens is given by the diagonal, usually in **inches**. One inch is 2.54 centimetres. In chess, too, the bishop always moves diagonally across the board. On garden gates and wooden frames, a diagonal brace stops the frame from twisting out of shape.

Solid shapes such as a cube have diagonals too. The **face diagonals** lie on the individual faces. The **space diagonals** run across the inside from one corner to the opposite one. A cube has four space diagonals, which all meet at the centre.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat shape with straight sides and several corners.
A shape with no corners dented inwards, in which all the diagonals lie inside.
Two corners joined by a side.
A unit of length of 2.54 centimetres, used to measure screens.

gewusst: A polygon with a hundred corners already has 4850 diagonals.
A hexagon has nine diagonals.
In a polygon that is not convex, a diagonal can even run outside the shape.

teile.einleitung: The Röstigraben (rösti ditch) is a joking name for the boundary between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland. It is not a real ditch, but the difference in language, culture and sometimes also in opinion at votes. The name comes from rösti, a typical potato dish of German-speaking Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Röstigraben refers to the language boundary between German and French in Switzerland.
It is named after rösti, which is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland.
The boundary runs roughly along the river Saane in Fribourg.
The cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Valais are bilingual.
Biel, in French Bienne, is the largest bilingual town in Switzerland.
In some votes, German-speaking Switzerland and the Romandie vote very differently.
In French people speak of the ‘rideau de rösti’, the rösti curtain.

abschnitte.text: The **Röstigraben** is an invisible line separating German-speaking Switzerland from the **Romandie**, the French-speaking west of the country. The name is a joke: rösti, a dish of grated and fried potatoes, originally comes from the canton of Bern and is seen as typical of German-speaking Switzerland. ‘Graben’ (ditch) means that there are sometimes differences between the two parts of the country. Today, however, rösti is eaten all over Switzerland. French speakers jokingly call the boundary the ‘rideau de rösti’, the rösti curtain.

The language boundary runs across Switzerland from the north-west to the south. In the Jura it runs between the French-speaking canton of Jura and the cantons of Basel-Landschaft and Solothurn. In the canton of Fribourg it roughly follows the river **Saane**, in French Sarine. In Valais it separates French-speaking Lower Valais from German-speaking **Upper Valais**, for example near Sierre and Leuk. That is why both language groups live together in the cantons of Bern, Fribourg and Valais.

Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. About 62 per cent of the population mainly speak German and about 23 per cent French (as of 2022). Most German-speaking Swiss speak dialect in everyday life, while in the Romandie French is spoken almost without dialect. At school, children learn a second **national language** so that people can understand each other. The boundary with Italian-speaking Ticino is sometimes jokingly called the **Polentagraben** (polenta ditch).

The Röstigraben becomes especially visible in some **popular votes**. A famous example is the vote on the European Economic Area, or EEA, in December 1992. The Romandie clearly voted yes, the majority of German-speaking Switzerland voted no, and so joining was rejected. Western Switzerland is often more open on questions about Europe and the welfare state. In many other votes, however, there is no big difference between the parts of the country.

Despite the ditch, the parts of the country hold together well, and many people are bilingual. The town of **Biel/Bienne** is a good example: street signs are written in both languages, and many people switch effortlessly between German and French. The town of Fribourg is also bilingual and has a bilingual university. School exchanges and language stays help people get to know the other culture. That is why many people see the variety of languages as a special treasure of Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: French-speaking western Switzerland.
A line where the area of one language ends and that of another begins.
One of the four official languages of Switzerland.
A vote in which those entitled to vote decide directly on an issue.

gewusst: In the past, rösti was a typical farmers' breakfast in Bern.
In Murten in the canton of Fribourg most people speak German, even though the canton is mainly French-speaking.
The Röstigraben even has an entry in dictionaries and is also used as a word in French.

teile.einleitung: The Sonderbund War was a short civil war in Switzerland in November 1847. It was the last war fought on Swiss soil. It led in 1848 to the modern Swiss federal state with a Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: The Sonderbund War took place in November 1847.
Seven Catholic-conservative cantons had joined together to form the Sonderbund (separate alliance).
They were opposed by the liberal cantons, who wanted a stronger confederation.
General Guillaume-Henri Dufour led the troops of the Diet.
The war lasted less than a month and had relatively few deaths.
It was the last war on Swiss soil.
Its direct result was the founding of the federal state with the Federal Constitution of 1848.

abschnitte.text: Before 1848 Switzerland was a loose **confederation of states** made up of cantons. Their joint assembly was called the **Diet** (Tagsatzung), and it had little power. The liberal cantons wanted a strong federal state and more freedoms. The Catholic-conservative cantons wanted to protect their independence and their religion.

In 1845 seven cantons formed a defensive alliance, the **Sonderbund**. It included Lucerne, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug, Fribourg and Valais. One trigger was that Lucerne had brought Jesuits into its schools, which outraged many liberals. In 1847 the Diet declared the Sonderbund incompatible with the Federal Treaty and demanded that it be dissolved.

Because the Sonderbund did not dissolve, war broke out in November 1847. The troops of the Diet were led by **General Guillaume-Henri Dufour** from Geneva. He wanted as few casualties as possible and ordered that prisoners and the wounded be treated well. Fribourg surrendered first, then the battle at Gisikon near Lucerne was decisive, and by the end of November the war was over.
The war lasted less than a month. On both sides together, about a hundred people died. Compared with other civil wars, this was very few. This was mainly thanks to Dufour's careful leadership.

After the war a new **Federal Constitution** was quickly drawn up, and it came into force in September 1848. The confederation of states became a federal state with a Federal Council, a National Council and a Council of States. Bern became the seat of government and parliament. The losers were not humiliated, which is one reason why Switzerland grew back together afterwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: A war between groups within the same country.
The assembly of representatives of the cantons before 1848.
A loose union of states that decide almost everything for themselves.
The most important law in Switzerland; it sets out how the state works and the rights of the people.

gewusst: The Sonderbund War was the last war fought in Switzerland.
General Dufour was also a cartographer: the Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif, the highest peak in Switzerland, is named after him.
Only a few months after the war, Switzerland had its first Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Colours are what our eyes see when light falls on something and is reflected back. White sunlight contains all the colours of the rainbow. Colours make our world bright, help animals to hide and warn, and can even affect our mood.
wichtigste: Colour is created by light that enters our eyes.
White light is made up of many colours, which you can see in a rainbow.
People usually count seven colours in a rainbow.
On a clear day the sky is blue because the air scatters blue light more strongly.
If you mix red and white, you get pink.
If you mix black and white, you get grey.
Our eyes contain cells that tell red, green and blue apart.

abschnitte.text: Light is a kind of wave, and each colour has its own **wavelength**. An object looks red because it mainly reflects red light and swallows the other colours. A white sheet of paper reflects all colours, a black one swallows almost all of them. So without light there are no colours; in the dark everything is black.

Around 1666 Isaac Newton showed with a **prism** that white light is made up of many colours. In a rainbow, raindrops act like lots of tiny prisms. People usually count seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. You only see a rainbow when the sun is behind you and rain is falling in front of you.

When painting with a paintbox you mix pigments; this is called **subtractive colour mixing**. Yellow and blue make green, red and yellow make orange. If you add white, a colour gets lighter, so red and white make pink. Black and white make grey.

Screens mix light instead of pigments; this is **additive colour mixing**. Every pixel is made of tiny red, green and blue lights. If all three shine equally brightly, you see white. In this way millions of different shades are created from just three colours.

In the retina of our eye there are sensory cells called **cones**. There are three kinds, which react especially to red, green or blue. In some people one kind of cone works differently; this is called **colour vision deficiency**. About eight in a hundred men, but only very few women, find it hard to tell red and green apart.

Colours give us important signals, for example red for stop and green for go at traffic lights. Animals use colours to hide, like the mountain hare, or to warn, like the wasp. Flags and coats of arms are also recognised by their colours, such as the red and white of Switzerland. Some people find blue calming and red exciting.

begriffe.erklaerung: A property of light that decides which colour we see.
A piece of glass that splits white light into its colours.
Sensory cells in the eye with which we see colours.
Basic colours from which many other colours can be mixed.

gewusst: Many dogs see the world mainly in shades of blue and yellow and can hardly tell red and green apart.
Mantis shrimps have far more kinds of colour-sensing cells than humans.
Sunsets are red because the light then travels an especially long way through the air and the blue is scattered away on the way.

teile.einleitung: Ruth Dreifuss is a Swiss politician who was the second woman elected to the Federal Council. In 1999 she became the first female President of the Swiss Confederation. She was also the first Jewish member of the national government.
wichtigste: Ruth Dreifuss was born in St Gallen on 9 January 1940.
She belongs to the Social Democratic Party, the SP for short.
In 1993 she became the second woman, after Elisabeth Kopp, to be elected to the Federal Council.
In 1999 she was the first female President of the Swiss Confederation.
From 1993 to 2002 she headed the Federal Department of Home Affairs.
Compulsory health insurance was introduced while she was in office.
She was the first Jewish member of the Federal Council.

abschnitte.text: Ruth Dreifuss was born in **St Gallen** on 9 January 1940 and grew up in Geneva. Her family was Jewish, and she later became the first Jewish member of the **Federal Council**. She first worked as a secretary and social worker, and later studied economics at the University of Geneva. After that she worked for Swiss development cooperation. From 1981 to 1993 she was a central secretary at the **Swiss Trade Union Federation**.

In 1993 one of the SP's seats on the Federal Council had to be filled. The party proposed **Christiane Brunner** from Geneva, but parliament elected a man, Francis Matthey. There were big protests, especially from women, who had waited many years for fair representation. Matthey turned down the office, and on 10 March 1993 Ruth Dreifuss was elected. This made her only the second woman in the national government, after Elisabeth Kopp, who had been elected in 1984.

abschnitte.titel: Her work on the Federal Council
abschnitte.text: Ruth Dreifuss headed the **Federal Department of Home Affairs**, which is responsible for health, social insurance and culture, among other things. During her time in office the new **Health Insurance Act** came into force in 1996; since then everyone in Switzerland has had to be insured against illness. She also worked for the AVS, the old-age pension for everyone. In drug policy she supported new approaches that offered help for addicts as well as punishment. She also wanted maternity leave for all working women, but it was only approved by the people in 2004.

The **President of the Confederation** is chosen every year from among the seven members of the Federal Council. In 1999 Ruth Dreifuss took on this office as the first woman in Swiss history. The President chairs the meetings of the Federal Council and represents Switzerland on important occasions. But she has no more power than the other members of the Federal Council. At the end of 2002 Ruth Dreifuss stepped down from the Federal Council.

Ruth Dreifuss is regarded as a pioneer for women in Swiss politics. Considering that women have only been allowed to vote at federal level since 1971, her election was an important step. Since then many women have sat on the Federal Council, and in 2010 it even had a female majority for a time. After her time in government, Dreifuss became active internationally, for example in a commission that campaigns for a new worldwide **drug policy**. She lives in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: The government of Switzerland, made up of seven members.
The member of the Federal Council who chairs it for one year and represents Switzerland in a special way.
A ministry, that is a part of the government with particular tasks.
Insurance that pays the costs of illness and visits to the doctor.

gewusst: When she was elected to the Federal Council, Ruth Dreifuss was not a member of parliament, which is rather rare.
At her election in 1993 many women carried flowers and placards in front of the Federal Palace to demonstrate for more women in government.
The events surrounding her election in 1993 have gone down in Swiss history as the ‘Brunner effect’.

teile.einleitung: Vostok Station is a Russian research station in the middle of the ice of Antarctica. On 21 July 1983 a temperature of minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was recorded there, the lowest air temperature ever measured at a weather station. Hidden beneath the station there is also a huge lake under the ice.
wichtigste: Vostok Station is in East Antarctica.
It was founded by the Soviet Union in 1957 and is run by Russia today.
On 21 July 1983 minus 89.2 degrees Celsius was measured there.
This is the lowest air temperature ever recorded at a weather station.
The station lies at about 3500 metres on the ice sheet.
Beneath it lies Lake Vostok, one of the largest lakes under the ice.
Ice cores reveal the climate of past hundreds of thousands of years.

abschnitte.text: The station lies in the interior of **East Antarctica**, far from any coast. It stands on a thick ice sheet, about 3500 metres above sea level. It is about 1300 kilometres to the South Pole. It is named after the ship Vostok, in which Russian sailors explored Antarctica around 1820. Vostok means east in Russian.

On 21 July 1983, in the middle of the Antarctic winter, the thermometer fell to **minus 89.2 degrees Celsius**. This is the lowest air temperature ever measured at a weather station. It is extremely cold there at other times too: the average temperature over the year is about minus 55 degrees. In winter the sun does not rise for months: it is the **polar night**. Satellites have even detected colder surfaces at other places in East Antarctica.

In winter only a few researchers and technicians live at the station, a few more in summer. The thin air at this altitude makes breathing and working hard. Supplies and fuel are brought from the coast by **sledge trains** pulled by tracked vehicles. Outside, people may only work for short periods and in thick protective clothing.

Near the station, researchers have drilled deep into the ice and brought up long **ice cores**. Tiny air bubbles from earlier times are trapped in the layers of ice. From them you can tell how warm it used to be and how much carbon dioxide was in the air. The Vostok ice core shows the climate of the last 400,000 years or so. The University of Bern is also world-famous for its research on ice cores like these.

About four kilometres below the station lies **Lake Vostok**, a lake of liquid water. It is about 250 kilometres long and has been cut off from the outside world for a very long time. It does not freeze because of the pressure of the ice and the heat from the Earth's interior. In 2012 a Russian drilling project reached its water for the first time. Researchers hope to find special living things there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The area around the South Pole, which is almost entirely covered with ice.
A base where scientists live and carry out studies.
A long rod of ice drilled out of the ice to study earlier times.
The time in winter when the sun does not rise at all near the poles.

gewusst: At minus 89 degrees, hot water thrown into the air would freeze into ice crystals at once.
By area, Lake Vostok is more than 20 times the size of Lake Constance.
Building the station began in 1957, during the International Geophysical Year, when many countries explored Antarctica together.

teile.einleitung: Pluto is a small, icy body far out at the edge of our solar system. After its discovery in 1930 it was considered the ninth planet for 76 years. In 2006, however, it was given a new status: since then Pluto has been a dwarf planet.
wichtigste: Pluto was discovered in 1930 by the American Clyde Tombaugh.
In 2006 the International Astronomical Union declared Pluto a dwarf planet.
It is smaller than our moon and has a diameter of about 2380 kilometres.
Pluto takes about 248 years to go once round the sun.
Pluto has five known moons; the largest is called Charon.
In 2015 the space probe New Horizons flew past Pluto and sent back the first close-up pictures.
On its surface there is a bright, heart-shaped plain of ice.

abschnitte.text: Astronomers had long suspected that there was another planet beyond Neptune. At the **Lowell Observatory** in Flagstaff in the USA, the young **Clyde Tombaugh** compared photos of the starry sky for months. In February 1930 he discovered a small point of light moving among the stars. The name Pluto was suggested by eleven-year-old **Venetia Burney** from England. In Roman mythology Pluto is the god of the underworld.

From the 1990s researchers discovered more and more icy bodies far out that are similar in size to Pluto. This region is called the **Kuiper Belt**. In 2005 Eris was found, which is almost exactly the same size as Pluto. So in 2006 in Prague the International Astronomical Union laid down what a planet is. A planet must have cleared its orbit of other bodies, which Pluto has not done, so since then it has been regarded as a **dwarf planet**.

On average Pluto is about 40 times as far from the sun as the Earth, that is about 6 billion kilometres. At around minus 230 degrees Celsius it is extremely cold there. Its surface consists of frozen nitrogen, methane and water ice that is as hard as rock. A day on Pluto lasts more than six Earth days. Its orbit is very elliptical, so that at times it is even closer to the sun than Neptune.

Pluto has five known moons: **Charon**, Nix, Hydra, Kerberos and Styx. Charon is more than half the size of Pluto itself. The two revolve around each other in such a way that they always show each other the same side. That is why some experts almost describe them as a double system. The smaller moons were only discovered from 2005 onwards with the Hubble Space Telescope.

In 2006 NASA's space probe **New Horizons** set off towards Pluto. After a journey of more than nine years it flew past it on 14 July 2015. It sent back razor-sharp pictures of mountains of water ice and wide plains of ice. A bright, heart-shaped region became especially famous; it is called **Tombaugh Regio** after the discoverer. On board the probe there is even a small amount of Clyde Tombaugh's ashes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round body that circles the sun but has not cleared its orbit.
A region beyond Neptune with a great many icy bodies.
The path on which one body circles another.
An uncrewed spacecraft that explores other bodies in space.

gewusst: Since its discovery in 1930, Pluto has not yet gone all the way round the sun even once.
Sunlight takes several hours to reach Pluto, but only about eight minutes to reach the Earth.
The cartoon character Pluto, Mickey Mouse's dog, got his name shortly after the discovery of the dwarf planet.

teile.einleitung: Probability tells us how good the chances are that something will happen. It helps with dice games, weather forecasts and even the lottery. For example, with two fair dice you roll a total of 7 with a probability of 1/6.
wichtigste: Probability always lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
It can be given as a fraction, as a decimal or as a percentage.
Often you calculate: favourable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes.
With a fair die, each number has a probability of 1/6.
With two dice, a total of 7 is the most common; its probability is 1/6.
The Basel mathematician Jakob Bernoulli was an important pioneer of probability theory.
Dice and coins have no memory.

abschnitte.text: Probability is a number that tells you how certain it is that an **event** will happen. A 0 means it never happens; a 1 means it is completely certain to happen. If you toss a coin, the chance of heads is 1/2, or 50 per cent. If you roll a die, the chance of a six is 1/6, or about 17 per cent.

In fair games you count the **favourable outcomes** and divide them by all possible outcomes. With two dice there are 6 times 6, that is 36, different rolls. A total of 7 comes from 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4, 4 and 3, 5 and 2, and 6 and 1. That is 6 out of 36 outcomes, so 1/6. A total of 2, on the other hand, only comes from two ones, so its probability is 1/36.

The **weather forecast** might say, for example: 70 per cent chance of rain. This means that on days like this it usually rains, but not always. In the Swiss Lotto you have to pick 6 out of 42 numbers and a lucky number correctly. The chance of winning the jackpot is about 1 in 31 million, which is tiny. Insurance companies also calculate with probabilities to set their prices.

In 1654 the Frenchmen **Blaise Pascal** and Pierre de Fermat wrote each other letters about games of chance. In doing so they laid the foundations of probability theory. Afterwards **Jakob Bernoulli** from Basel wrote a famous book about it, which appeared in 1713. It contains the law of large numbers: the more often you roll the dice, the closer the results get to the calculated probabilities.

Many people believe that after red has come up five times in roulette, black must finally come up now. That is not true, because the ball knows nothing about the earlier spins. This mistake is called the **gambler's fallacy**. Another surprise: with just 23 people in a room, the chance that two of them share a birthday is greater than 50 per cent.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can happen in an experiment, for example rolling a six.
Something happens without anyone being able to know exactly beforehand.
Means out of a hundred, so 50 per cent is half.
A fair die or a fair coin does not favour any result.

gewusst: The probability of winning the jackpot in the Swiss Lotto is smaller than that of being struck by lightning.
With just 23 people in a room, there is a more than 50 per cent probability that two of them share a birthday.
The Bernoulli family from Basel produced several famous mathematicians.

teile.einleitung: The Día de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is a big festival in Mexico. At the beginning of November, families joyfully remember their relatives who have died. Colourful sugar skulls, orange flowers and decorated altars are all part of it.
wichtigste: The Día de los Muertos is celebrated mainly in Mexico.
The most important days of the festival are 1 and 2 November.
People believe that the souls of the dead come to visit on these days.
Families build altars at home with photos, food and flowers.
Colourful sugar skulls and orange marigolds are typical.
The festival is cheerful and colourful, not sad.
UNESCO counts it as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

abschnitte.titel: A cheerful festival of the dead
abschnitte.text: On the Día de los Muertos people remember grandparents, parents and friends who have died. Unlike many festivals of the dead in Europe, there is laughing, eating, singing and music. People believe that the **souls** of the dead return to their families for a short time. On 1 November people often think of children who have died, and on 2 November of adults.

In many homes people build a decorated altar called an **ofrenda**. On it they place photos of the dead, candles and their favourite food and drinks. A sweet bread, the **pan de muerto**, must not be missing. The offerings are meant to welcome the souls after their long journey.

Bright orange **marigolds**, called cempasúchil in Spanish, decorate altars and graves. Their scent and colour are meant to show the souls the way. Colourful sugar skulls, the **calaveras**, often carry the names of living or dead people. Garlands of cut paper in many colours also hang everywhere.

Many families clean and decorate the graves of their relatives. In some places they spend the whole night at the cemetery with candles, music and food. The island of Janitzio and the area around Lake Pátzcuaro, for example, are known for this. The cemeteries then glow like a sea of lights.

The roots of the festival go far back to the **Aztecs** and other ancient peoples of Mexico. After the Spanish arrived, it became linked with the Christian holidays of All Saints’ Day and All Souls’ Day. The elegant skeleton lady **La Catrina** goes back to a drawing by the artist José Guadalupe Posada from around 1910. Today many people dress up as Catrina and paint their faces like a skull.

In 2008 UNESCO added the festival to the list of **intangible cultural heritage**. It is also celebrated in a big way in the USA, where many people of Mexican origin live. Since 2016 there has been a big parade in Mexico City, inspired by a James Bond film. The 2017 animated film Coco made the festival known to children all over the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A decorated altar with offerings for the dead.
A skull, often made of sugar or chocolate and brightly decorated.
Mexican name of the orange marigold, the flower of the dead.
Christian day of remembrance for the dead on 2 November.

gewusst: The sugar skulls are not necessarily eaten; they are often mainly for decoration.
In Mexico people write funny poems for the festival about living people as if they had already died, and these are also called calaveras.
The big parade in Mexico City only began after it had been shown in a film.

teile.einleitung: At 4634 metres, the Dufourspitze is the highest mountain peak in Switzerland. It belongs to the Monte Rosa massif in the canton of Valais, very close to the border with Italy. It is named after General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, who made the first accurate map of Switzerland.
wichtigste: At 4634 metres, the Dufourspitze is the highest peak in Switzerland.
It lies in the Monte Rosa massif in the canton of Valais.
The summit is only a few hundred metres from the border with Italy.
After Mont Blanc it is the second-highest mountain in the Alps.
It is named after the general and map-maker Guillaume-Henri Dufour.
It was first climbed on 1 August 1855.
Climbs usually start from Zermatt and the Monte Rosa Hut.

abschnitte.text: The Dufourspitze rises in the south of the canton of **Valais**, east of Zermatt. It is the highest peak of the mighty **Monte Rosa massif**, which lies on the border between Switzerland and Italy. The summit itself stands just on Swiss soil. The highest mountain lying entirely in Switzerland, on the other hand, is the Dom at 4545 metres.

Around Monte Rosa lie large glaciers, such as the **Gorner Glacier**, one of the biggest glaciers in the Alps. Because of global warming, the glaciers are melting and getting shorter every year. At this height the air is thin and cold, and it can snow even in summer. Hardly any plants grow up here any more.

In the past the peak was simply called Höchste Spitze, “highest peak”. In 1863 the **Federal Council** named it after Guillaume-Henri Dufour. Dufour was general in the Sonderbund War of 1847 and one of the founders of the Red Cross. Under his leadership the first accurate national map of Switzerland was made, the **Dufour Map**.

On 1 August 1855 a roped party reached the summit for the first time. It was made up of several Englishmen and mountain guides from Valais and the Bernese Oberland. At that time there were neither huts nor modern equipment. The first ascent fell in the **Golden Age of Alpinism**, when many four-thousanders were climbed for the first time.

Most mountaineers start at the **Monte Rosa Hut** at about 2880 metres. From there the climb takes many hours over glaciers and an exposed rocky ridge. The route is only for experienced mountaineers with rope, crampons and ice axe, or with a mountain guide. The modern hut opened in 2009 and produces much of its own electricity from solar energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of mountains that belong closely together.
A mountain at least 4000 metres high.
A large river of ice that flows slowly down the valley.
A group of climbers joined together by a rope.
The first time people reach a summit.

gewusst: The first ascent took place, of all days, on 1 August, which is today the Swiss national holiday.
On the Italian side of Monte Rosa, at over 4500 metres, stands the Capanna Margherita, one of the highest huts in Europe.
The Dufourspitze is only 174 metres lower than Mont Blanc, the highest mountain in the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Radiocarbon dating is a method for working out the age of old bones, wood or fabrics. It measures how much radioactive carbon, known as carbon-14, is still left in an object. This is how researchers know, for example, that the glacier mummy Ötzi lived more than 5000 years ago.
wichtigste: Radiocarbon dating is also called the C14 method.
It only works on things that were once alive, such as wood, bone or fabric made from plant fibres.
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years.
After about 11,460 years only a quarter of the original carbon-14 is left.
With this method ages of up to about 50,000 years can be determined.
It was invented by the American Willard Libby, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960.
ETH Zurich also runs a well-known laboratory for this kind of dating.

abschnitte.text: Carbon is an element found in all living things. Almost all carbon is the stable carbon-12, but a tiny part is **carbon-14**, or C14 for short. C14 is constantly formed high up in the atmosphere when radiation from space hits nitrogen. It is **radioactive**, which means its atoms decay again over time. Plants take in C14 from the air, and animals and people through their food.

As long as a living thing is alive, it keeps taking in new carbon, and the proportion of C14 stays the same. When it dies, no new carbon is added, and the C14 slowly decays. After about 5730 years only half is left; this is called the **half-life**. After two half-lives, about 11,460 years, a quarter is left, and after three half-lives an eighth. If you measure how much C14 is still there, you can work out when the living thing died.

The American chemist **Willard Libby** developed the method in the late 1940s. He tested it on objects whose age was already known, such as wood from Egyptian tombs. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it in 1960. Later it was found that the C14 content of the air had not always been the same in the past. That is why the results are now compared with the **tree rings** of very old trees to make them more accurate.

The glacier mummy **Ötzi** was found in the Ötztal Alps in 1991. Radiocarbon dating showed that he lived about 5300 years ago. In 1988 three laboratories, including one at ETH Zurich, examined the famous **Shroud of Turin**. All three concluded that the cloth dates from the Middle Ages. Cave paintings, pile dwellings on Swiss lakes and ancient scrolls have also been dated in this way.

Radiocarbon dating only works on material that was once alive. Stones, metals or dinosaur bones that have turned to stone cannot be dated with it. After about 50,000 years so little C14 is left that it can hardly be measured. For very old finds, researchers therefore use other methods. Today, thanks to modern devices called **accelerator mass spectrometers**, only tiny samples of a few milligrams are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time after which half of a radioactive substance has decayed.
When atomic nuclei decay by themselves and give off radiation.
A variant of an element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons.
Working out how old something is.
