Further up come cereals, dairy products, meat, fish or eggs. Sweets and snacks are right at the top, and you should only eat a little of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Substances in food that the body needs for energy and growth.
Important substances that you only need in small amounts, found for example in fruit and vegetables.
A ceramic pot in which fondue is made.
A small snack in the morning.

gewusst: You need about twelve litres of milk to make one kilogram of hard cheese.
A single bee produces only about a teaspoon of honey in its whole life.
The expression ‘Röstigraben’ (rösti ditch) refers to the boundary between German-speaking and French-speaking Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Colosseum is a huge amphitheatre in the centre of Rome. Almost 2000 years ago, gladiator fights and animal hunts took place here in front of tens of thousands of spectators. Today it is the best-known building from the time of ancient Rome.
wichtigste: The Colosseum was built from about AD 72 under the Emperor Vespasian.
The Emperor Titus opened it in AD 80 with 100 days of games.
It had room for about 50,000 spectators.
Gladiator fights took place in the Colosseum.
Animal hunts and executions were also part of the shows.
Its Latin name is Amphitheatrum Flavium.
In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

abschnitte.text: The Colosseum is an **amphitheatre**, an oval building with rows of seats rising all the way round. It is about 188 metres long, 156 metres wide and around 48 metres high. It was built mainly from travertine, tuff, bricks and concrete. It probably got the name Colosseum from a gigantic statue of the Emperor Nero that stood next to it.

The Emperor **Vespasian** had building work begin around AD 72, on the site of an artificial lake from Nero's palace grounds. His son Titus opened the theatre in the year 80 with games that lasted 100 days. It was completed under the Emperor Domitian. Because these emperors belonged to the Flavian family, the building was called the Amphitheatrum Flavium.

The **gladiators** were fighters, often slaves, prisoners of war or convicts, who fought each other to entertain the audience. There were different types, for example the net fighter with a trident. In the **animal hunts**, people fought wild animals such as lions, bears or elephants from distant lands. Entry was usually free for citizens, because the emperors wanted to make themselves popular with the people.

Beneath the arena lay the **hypogeum**, a maze of passages and cages. With lifts and trapdoors, animals and scenery could suddenly appear in the arena. When the sun was out, sailors stretched a gigantic awning, the velarium, over the spectators. Through 80 entrances people could get in and out quickly.

After the games ended in the 6th century, the Colosseum slowly fell into ruin. Earthquakes damaged it, and in the Middle Ages it served as a **quarry** for other buildings in Rome. Today it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage and is visited by millions of people every year. There were Roman amphitheatres in Switzerland too, for example in Avenches and in Windisch.

begriffe.erklaerung: An oval or round open-air theatre with rows of seats all round.
A fighter in ancient Rome who fought to entertain the audience.
The fighting area in the middle, originally covered with sand.
Underground passages and rooms beneath the arena.

gewusst: The word arena comes from the Latin word for sand, which covered the ground.
The holes you see everywhere in the walls today come from metal clamps that were broken out in the Middle Ages.
The Colosseum is shown on the Italian 5-cent coin.

teile.einleitung: Malala Yousafzai is a Pakistani campaigner for girls' right to education. As a teenager she survived an attack because she wanted to go to school. In 2014, at the age of 17, she became the youngest person ever to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
wichtigste: Malala was born on 12 July 1997 in Mingora in the Swat Valley in Pakistan.
She campaigns for all girls to be allowed to go to school.
In 2012 Taliban fighters shot her in the head; she survived with severe injuries.
She was treated in Birmingham in England and then lived there.
In 2014, aged 17, she received the Nobel Peace Prize.
She founded the Malala Fund for girls' education.
In 2020 she completed a degree at the University of Oxford.

abschnitte.text: Malala grew up in the **Swat Valley** in north-western Pakistan. Her father Ziauddin ran a school and encouraged her to learn a lot. From about 2007 the radical **Taliban** took more and more power in the region. They banned girls from going to school and destroyed many schools.

At the beginning of 2009, Malala, only eleven years old, wrote a **diary** for the BBC under a false name. In it she described what life was like under the Taliban and how much she missed school. Later she also spoke openly on television about the right to education. This made her known in Pakistan, but also put her in danger.

On 9 October 2012 a Taliban fighter stopped her school bus and shot Malala in the head. Two of her friends were also injured. Malala was flown to **Birmingham** in England and operated on several times there. She recovered and went on living in England with her family.

On her 16th birthday in 2013 Malala gave a speech at the **United Nations** in New York. Since then 12 July has also been called Malala Day. In 2014 she received the **Nobel Peace Prize** together with the Indian Kailash Satyarthi, who fights against child labour. At 17 she was the youngest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize.

Together with her father she founded the **Malala Fund**, which aims to make it possible for girls all over the world to go to school. Her book ‘I Am Malala’ appeared in 2013 and was translated into many languages. In 2020 she completed a degree in philosophy, politics and economics at the University of **Oxford**. She says that one child, one teacher, one book and one pen can change the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A radical armed group that enforces strict rules in parts of Afghanistan and Pakistan.
An important award for people who work for peace.
Everything you learn at school and in life.
An organisation of almost all the states in the world, the UN for short.

gewusst: Malala was named after Malalai, an Afghan folk heroine.
She was presented with her Nobel Prize in Oslo on 10 December 2014.
According to UNESCO estimates, around 120 million girls worldwide do not go to school (as of about 2023).

teile.einleitung: The CRISPR/Cas method is a tool with which researchers can change the genetic material of living things very precisely. That is why it is also called gene scissors. For developing it, Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
wichtigste: CRISPR/Cas9 is a pair of gene scissors that can cut DNA at a particular place.
Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna presented the method in 2012.
For this the two researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
The idea comes from bacteria, which use it to defend themselves against viruses.
The method is used in medicine, agriculture and research.
Since 2023 there has been a first approved medicine based on CRISPR.
Changing the genetic material of humans raises difficult ethical questions.

abschnitte.text: Every living thing carries a building plan in its cells, its **DNA**. With the gene scissors CRISPR/Cas9 you can cut this plan open at a precisely chosen place. The cell can then remove a piece, change it or put in a new piece. You can picture it like the find-and-replace function in a word processor.

The method has two parts. A small piece of **guide RNA** looks for the right place in the genetic material, like an address label. The protein **Cas9** is the actual pair of scissors and cuts through the DNA there. The cell then repairs the cut itself, and in doing so the desired change is made.

Originally CRISPR is a defence system that **bacteria** use against viruses. The bacteria store small pieces of the viruses’ genetic material, as if in a book of wanted criminals. If the same virus attacks again, they recognise it and cut up its genetic material. Japanese researchers discovered the strange repeats in bacterial DNA as early as 1987, but their meaning was only understood much later.

The Frenchwoman **Emmanuelle Charpentier** and the American **Jennifer Doudna** showed in 2012 that the bacterial system can be used as a tool. Their work appeared in the scientific journal Science. Just eight years later they received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. It was the first time that two women together had won a Nobel Prize in a natural science.

In medicine there is hope of curing inherited diseases. At the end of 2023 a first medicine against **sickle cell disease** that works with CRISPR was approved in Great Britain and the USA. In agriculture, plants are being developed that cope better with drought or diseases. In laboratories all over the world, gene scissors are now an everyday tool.

Because CRISPR could also be used to change the genetic material of embryos, there are strict rules. In 2018 a researcher in China changed the genetic material of babies and was convicted for it. In Switzerland, growing genetically modified plants has been banned by a moratorium since a **popular vote** in 2005. Experts and politicians are discussing how to deal responsibly with the new possibilities.

begriffe.erklaerung: The genetic material, the building plan in every cell of a living thing.
A section of DNA that controls a particular feature.
A protein that cuts through DNA like a pair of scissors.
A ban or delay that applies for a certain time.

gewusst: CRISPR is an abbreviation of an English name that describes the repeated sections in the genetic material of bacteria.
The gene scissors are so cheap and simple that students already use them at many universities.
With CRISPR, for example, mushrooms have been bred that go brown less quickly after being cut.

teile.einleitung: The Jungfraujoch is a mountain saddle between the peaks of the Jungfrau and the Mönch in the Bernese Oberland. Here, at 3454 metres above sea level, is the highest railway station in Europe. Because of its location, the Jungfraujoch is also called the ‘Top of Europe’.
wichtigste: The Jungfraujoch lies between the Jungfrau and the Mönch on the border of the cantons of Bern and Valais.
Jungfraujoch station, at 3454 metres above sea level, is the highest railway station in Europe.
The Jungfrau Railway has run up from Kleine Scheidegg since 1912.
Most of the line runs through a tunnel inside the Eiger and the Mönch.
From the Jungfraujoch you can see the Great Aletsch Glacier.
On a rocky peak stands the Sphinx Observatory for research.
The region is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.

abschnitte.text: A **col** (in German ‘Joch’) is a dip between two mountain peaks. The Jungfraujoch lies between the Jungfrau at 4158 metres and the Mönch at 4107 metres. The famous Eiger is also very close by. The border between the cantons of Bern and Valais runs across the col.

The Zurich industrialist **Adolf Guyer-Zeller** had the idea for the railway in 1893. Construction took 16 years, and on 1 August 1912 the line to the Jungfraujoch was opened. The **rack railway** starts at Kleine Scheidegg and runs mostly through a tunnel more than 7 kilometres long. On the way there are stops with windows through which you look out of the Eiger North Face and onto the Eismeer (sea of ice).

South of the Jungfraujoch begins the **Great Aletsch Glacier**, the longest glacier in the Alps. It is about 20 kilometres long, but because of climate change it melts back a little every year. Since 2001 the region has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At this altitude there is snow almost all year round, and it can be below zero even in summer.

At 3571 metres stands the **Sphinx Observatory**, which you reach by lift. There and in the research station, experts measure the air, the weather and radiation from space. Because the air here is very clean, the place is well suited to observing changes in the atmosphere. The station is part of a worldwide network of measuring stations.

The Jungfraujoch is one of the most popular destinations in Switzerland and attracts visitors from all over the world. There is an **Ice Palace** with figures made of ice, viewing terraces and restaurants. Since 2020 the Eiger Express cable car from Grindelwald has shortened the journey time. Because the air is thin at this altitude, you should move slowly up there.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dip or crossing point between two mountain peaks.
A railway with a cogwheel and toothed rail that can manage very steep lines.
A large mass of ice that flows slowly down the valley.
A building for scientific observations, for example of the sky or the air.

gewusst: Originally the Jungfrau Railway was supposed to go all the way to the summit of the Jungfrau, but this plan was never carried out.
On the Jungfraujoch water boils at only about 88 degrees, because the air pressure is lower.
The founder Adolf Guyer-Zeller died in 1899 and did not live to see the whole line opened.

teile.einleitung: The Fibonacci sequence is a famous series of numbers: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on. Each number is the sum of the two numbers before it. Amazingly, this sequence turns up in many places in nature, for example in sunflowers and pine cones.
wichtigste: The Fibonacci sequence begins with 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.
Each new number is the sum of the two before it.
It is named after the mathematician Leonardo of Pisa, known as Fibonacci.
He described it in 1202 in his arithmetic book Liber Abaci with a problem about rabbits.
If you divide a Fibonacci number by the one before it, you get closer and closer to the golden ratio of about 1.618.
Fibonacci numbers can be found in the spirals of sunflowers and pine cones.

abschnitte.text: You start with 1 and 1. Then you add the last two numbers together: 1 plus 1 makes 2, 1 plus 2 makes 3, 2 plus 3 makes 5. And so it goes on: 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89. A rule like this, in which each number is calculated from the ones before, is called **recursive**.

**Leonardo of Pisa** lived in Italy from about 1170 to 1240. Because his father was a merchant, he travelled to North Africa and got to know the Hindu-Arabic numerals there. In his book **Liber Abaci** of 1202 he explained to Europeans how to calculate with these numerals, which we still use today. He only got the name Fibonacci, which means son of Bonacci, later.

In his book Fibonacci set a problem about how **rabbits** multiply. A young pair becomes adult after one month and then has a new pair every month. If you count the pairs month by month, you get exactly the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Real rabbits, of course, do not multiply quite so regularly.

The seeds of a **sunflower** form spirals that turn to the left and to the right. If you count them, you often find Fibonacci numbers such as 34 and 55, or 55 and 89. This pattern also appears in pine cones, pineapples and romanesco cauliflower. In this way plants make especially good use of the space.

If you divide a Fibonacci number by the one before it, for example 89 by 55, you get about 1.618. This special number is called the **golden ratio**. Many people find shapes in this proportion especially beautiful. That is why artists and architects have used it in pictures and buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A series of numbers that follow one another according to a certain rule.
The result when you add numbers together.
A special proportion of about 1 to 1.618.
A line that keeps winding round a central point.

gewusst: The sequence was known in India centuries before Fibonacci, there in connection with the metres of poems.
Many flowers have a Fibonacci number of petals, for example lilies have three and wild roses five.
The twelfth Fibonacci number is 144, which is exactly 12 times 12.

teile.einleitung: Deontological ethics, also called the ethics of duty, judges actions by whether they fulfil a duty. Its best-known representative is the German philosopher Immanuel Kant.
wichtigste: The Greek word ‘deon’ means what is required, or duty.
Some actions are required or forbidden in themselves, regardless of their consequences.
For Kant only a **good will** is good without limitation.
An action only has moral worth if it is done **from duty**.
Kant distinguishes between perfect and imperfect duties.
In 1930 W. D. Ross introduced prima facie duties.

abschnitte.text: **Deontology** is the study of duties. It asks which actions are required or forbidden. Unlike **consequentialist ethics**, such as utilitarianism, it does not look primarily at the result. A ban on lying then applies even if a lie would be useful at that moment. What matters is the action itself and whether it is **in accordance with duty**.

**Immanuel Kant** lived from 1724 to 1804 in Königsberg. In his ‘Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals’ he writes that only a **good will** is good without limitation. Talents, courage or wealth can also be used for evil. Kant defines duty as ‘the necessity of an action from respect for the law’. He means the moral law, which reason recognises.

Kant tells of a shopkeeper who gives children the correct change. But he only does this so that his shop has a good reputation. His action is **in accordance with duty**, but not done **from duty**. On the outside it matches the duty, but it is based on self-interest. For Kant an action only has moral worth if it is done out of respect for duty.

Kant distinguishes **perfect duties**, which apply without exception, such as the ban on lying, and **imperfect duties**, which leave room for choice, such as helping others in need. A dispute in 1797 shows how strict the ban on lying is. The French-Swiss writer **Benjamin Constant** asked whether you may lie to a murderer to save a friend. Kant replied with the essay ‘On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy’ and stuck to the ban.

Sometimes two duties contradict each other. That is why in 1930, in ‘The Right and the Good’, the British philosopher **William David Ross** proposed **prima facie duties**. They include fidelity, reparation and beneficence. They apply at first, but can be outweighed by a weightier duty. In this way people try to combine Kant's strictness with a view of the concrete situation.

gewusst: Kant hardly ever left his home town of Königsberg in his whole life.
Benjamin Constant was born in Lausanne.

teile.einleitung: Octopuses are sea creatures with eight arms and no bones. They are regarded as the cleverest invertebrates in the world. An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
wichtigste: Octopuses have eight arms with suckers.
They are molluscs and are related to snails and mussels.
An octopus has three hearts.
Their blood is blue because it contains copper instead of iron.
Octopuses can change colour in a flash and camouflage themselves.
When in danger, they squirt out a cloud of ink.
There are about 300 species of octopus.

abschnitte.text: Octopuses have a soft, bag-shaped body, the **mantle**, and eight arms with suckers. Their only hard body part is a beak-like mouth. That is why even large octopuses can squeeze through tiny openings. The common octopus grows to about one metre long, and the giant Pacific octopus can reach an arm span of several metres.

Two smaller hearts, the **gill hearts**, pump blood through the gills. The third heart supplies the rest of the body. The blood is blue because the oxygen is bound to the copper-containing pigment **haemocyanin**. When the octopus swims, the body heart stops beating at times, which is why octopuses prefer to crawl over the seabed.

Octopuses live in all the world's oceans, from shallow coasts to the deep sea. During the day they usually hide in rock crevices or caves. They mainly hunt crabs, mussels and fish. They crack shells with their beak, and some species paralyse their prey with **venom**.

Octopuses have about 500 million nerve cells, and a large part of them are in the arms. In experiments, octopuses opened screw-top jars and found their way through mazes. With special skin cells, the **chromatophores**, they can change colour and pattern in a fraction of a second. The mimic octopus even imitates other animals such as sea snakes or flatfish.

Most octopuses live only one to two years. The female lays thousands of eggs in a den and guards them for weeks or months without eating. Shortly after the young have hatched, the mother dies. Octopuses do not live in the wild in Switzerland because they only live in **salt water**, but you can see them in zoos and aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of molluscs that includes octopuses, cuttlefish and squid.
A round sticky disc with which the octopus holds on and feels things.
Skin cells containing pigment with which octopuses change their colour.
A copper-containing substance in the blood that carries oxygen and turns it blue.

gewusst: An octopus can taste with its suckers.
Paul the octopus from a German aquarium became famous in 2010 because he correctly predicted the German football team's matches at the World Cup.
If an octopus loses an arm, a new one can grow back.

teile.einleitung: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. As a by-product it produces the oxygen we need to breathe. You could say that photosynthesis is nature's kitchen, feeding almost all life on Earth.
wichtigste: In photosynthesis, plants turn light energy into chemical energy.
The starting materials are carbon dioxide and water.
The products are grape sugar, that is glucose, and oxygen.
For one molecule of glucose the plant needs 6 molecules of carbon dioxide and 6 molecules of water.
Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll.
Algae and some bacteria also carry out photosynthesis.
Without photosynthesis there would hardly be any oxygen in the air.

abschnitte.text: The word **photosynthesis** comes from Greek and means roughly ‘putting together with light’. Plants, algae and some bacteria use it to build energy-rich sugar out of simple substances. The energy for this comes from sunlight. The plants use the sugar to grow, or they store it as **starch**, for example in potatoes. Animals and people who eat plants indirectly use this stored solar energy.

Photosynthesis can be summed up in a chemical equation. 6 molecules of **carbon dioxide** and 6 molecules of water produce 1 molecule of **glucose** and 6 molecules of oxygen. In formulas this is written: 6 CO2 plus 6 H2O gives C6H12O6 plus 6 O2. Plants take in the carbon dioxide from the air through tiny openings in their leaves. The water comes from the soil through the roots.

Photosynthesis takes place in small green parts of plant cells, the **chloroplasts**. They contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green. In a first step, the light reaction, light energy is captured and water is split, producing oxygen. In a second step, the **Calvin cycle**, this energy is used to build carbon dioxide into sugar. The gases pass in and out through the stomata on the underside of the leaf.

In 1771 the Englishman **Joseph Priestley** showed that a plant ‘improves’ used air in a closed jar. In 1779 the Dutch doctor **Jan Ingenhousz** found out that plants need light to do this. In the 20th century the American Melvin Calvin worked out the individual steps of how sugar is built. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for this in 1961. Experts are still studying photosynthesis today, for example in order to make better use of solar energy.

Almost all food chains on Earth begin with photosynthesis. It provides the **oxygen** that people and animals need to breathe. A large part of it comes not from trees but from tiny algae in the sea, the plankton. Photosynthesis also removes carbon dioxide from the air and so helps to regulate the climate. Oil, natural gas and coal were also formed from plants and tiny organisms that carried out photosynthesis millions of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green leaf pigment that captures the light for photosynthesis.
A tiny part of a plant cell in which photosynthesis takes place.
A simple sugar, also called grape sugar, that supplies energy.
A tiny opening in a leaf through which gases flow in and out.

gewusst: In autumn the chlorophyll in the leaves breaks down, and the yellow and red pigments that were hidden before become visible.
Plants also breathe and use oxygen, especially at night, but during the day they produce much more than they use.
The oxygen produced in photosynthesis comes from the water and not from the carbon dioxide.

teile.einleitung: Geometric shapes are figures such as the circle, triangle or square and solids such as the cube or sphere. We find them all around us, from a football to a road sign. Geometry is the part of mathematics that deals with such shapes.
wichtigste: Flat shapes are called figures; three-dimensional shapes are called solids.
A square has four sides of equal length and four right angles.
A hexagon has six corners and six sides.
The stop sign has the shape of an octagon.
A dice has six square faces.
A completely round solid like a ball is called a sphere.
Shapes help us to build, measure and design.

abschnitte.text: A **geometric shape** is defined by points, lines and surfaces. Figures such as the triangle, rectangle and circle are flat and lie in a plane. A **solid**, on the other hand, has length, width and height, for example a cube, a pyramid or a cylinder. More than 2000 years ago the Greek mathematician Euclid wrote a famous book about geometry.

Figures with straight sides are called **polygons**. A triangle has three corners, a quadrilateral four, a pentagon five and a hexagon six. A square is a special quadrilateral with four sides of equal length and four right angles. A rectangle also has four right angles, but its sides are not necessarily all the same length.

In a **circle**, all the points on the edge are the same distance from the centre. This distance is called the radius. The circumference of a circle is always a little more than three times as long as its diameter; this number is called pi. The **sphere** is the three-dimensional counterpart of the circle, like a ball or a marble.

A **cube** is made of six squares of the same size and has eight corners and twelve edges. A box or a brick is a cuboid. Tins and pipes are cylinders, and an ice cream cone has the shape of a cone. The famous pyramids in Egypt have a square base and four triangular sides.

Bees build their honeycombs from **hexagons**, because this shape needs little wax and is very stable. Many snowflakes have six arms. Road signs have particular shapes so that you recognise them quickly: the stop sign is an octagon, and warning signs in Switzerland are triangles. The classic football is stitched together from pentagons and hexagons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flat shape such as a triangle or a circle.
A three-dimensional shape with length, width and height, for example a cube.
An angle like the corner of a table; it measures 90 degrees.
The line where two faces of a solid meet.
A number of about 3.14 that shows how much longer the circumference of a circle is than its diameter.

gewusst: The classic football is made of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
On a dice, the dots on opposite sides always add up to 7.
For the same volume, the sphere is the solid with the smallest surface, which is why soap bubbles are round.

teile.einleitung: The Congress of Vienna was a large meeting of European rulers and diplomats in 1814 and 1815. After Napoleon's downfall, the map of Europe was redrawn there. It was especially important for Switzerland, because the great powers recognised its perpetual neutrality.
wichtigste: The Congress of Vienna took place from September 1814 to June 1815.
It reorganised Europe after the Napoleonic Wars.
It was led by the Austrian statesman Prince Metternich.
The great powers recognised Switzerland's perpetual neutrality.
Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel joined Switzerland as new cantons.
The canton of Bern received most of the Jura.
The congress was followed by a long period without major wars in Europe.

abschnitte.text: After the victory over **Napoleon**, emperors, kings and diplomats met in **Vienna** from September 1814. The most important powers were Austria, Russia, Prussia and Great Britain. Later the defeated France was also allowed a say, represented by the skilful diplomat Talleyrand. The host and leader was the Austrian foreign minister **Klemens von Metternich**.

The participants wanted to restore the old ruling houses and create a **balance** of power. No country was ever again to become as strong as France had been under Napoleon. Instead of the old Empire, the German Confederation was created. Many borders were redrawn without asking the people.

Alongside the negotiations there were many splendid balls, concerts and parties in Vienna. That is why people said mockingly: the congress dances, but it makes no progress. In March 1815 Napoleon escaped from the island of Elba and returned to France. Only after his final defeat at **Waterloo** in June 1815 was the danger over. The Final Act of the congress was signed on 9 June 1815.

At the Congress of Vienna, the great powers recognised Switzerland's perpetual **neutrality**, set down in a document signed in Paris in November 1815. Geneva, Valais and Neuchâtel became new cantons, so that Switzerland now had 22 cantons. The canton of Bern received most of the **Jura** in return for territories in Aargau and Vaud. The Valtellina, which had previously belonged to the Grisons, did not come back, however. These Swiss borders are essentially still valid today.

After the congress there was no major war between the powers in Europe for a long time. The period that followed is called the **Restoration**, because the old order was restored. But many people wanted freedom and a say in government, which led to uprisings, for example in 1848. Even so, the Congress of Vienna is regarded as an example of how states can create peace through negotiation.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large assembly at which important questions are discussed.
A country stays out of other countries' wars and does not take sides.
A person who represents a country in negotiations with other countries.
The re-establishment of an old order, here the return of the former rulers.

gewusst: Charles Pictet de Rochemont from Geneva negotiated successfully for Switzerland in Vienna and Paris.
The congress never met together in one large hall; the most important decisions were made in small groups.
As a result of the Congress of Vienna, the Prince-Bishopric of Basel lost its independence and mostly went to Bern.

teile.einleitung: When a person dies, relatives and friends say goodbye at a funeral. Depending on the country, religion and family, this farewell looks very different, but everywhere it is about remembering and mourning.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the funeral service is often called an **Abdankung**.
In a cremation the ashes are placed in an **urn**.
In Switzerland today the great majority choose cremation.
Catholic Christians remember the dead on All Souls' Day, 2 November.
In Judaism people place small stones on a grave.
In Islam the dead person is laid with their face towards Mecca.
In Mexico people celebrate the colourful ‘Día de los Muertos’.

abschnitte.text: A funeral helps the living to say goodbye. In Switzerland the funeral service is often called an **Abdankung**. During it, relatives, a minister or a funeral speaker remember the life of the person who has died. There is often music, flowers and candles. Afterwards many people meet for a meal together.

In a **burial**, the dead person is laid in a coffin in the grave. In a **cremation**, the body is burned in a **crematorium**, and the ashes are placed in an **urn**. In Switzerland today the great majority choose cremation. The urn can be placed in a grave or in a **columbarium**, a wall with niches. In Switzerland the cantons and municipalities regulate funeral matters.

In Christianity there are two days of remembrance in November: **All Saints' Day** on 1 November and **All Souls' Day** on 2 November. Many people then visit graves and light candles. In **Judaism** the dead person is buried in the earth as soon as possible. Anyone visiting a grave often places a small stone on it. It shows that someone was there and is thinking of the person.

In **Islam** the body is washed, wrapped in cloths and buried in the earth as quickly as possible. The face is turned towards **Mecca**. In **Hinduism** the dead are usually cremated. Many Hindus give the ashes to the **Ganges**, which is regarded as a holy river. The city of **Varanasi** in India is especially well known for this.

abschnitte.titel: A colourful festival of the dead
abschnitte.text: In **Mexico**, at the beginning of November, people celebrate the **Día de los Muertos**, the Day of the Dead. Families build altars with photos, candles and orange flowers. Sugar skulls are part of it too. People believe that the dead come to visit on these days. UNESCO counts the festival as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity.

gewusst: The word columbarium comes from the Latin ‘columba’, dove, because the niches look like dovecotes.
At the Mexican Day of the Dead, people do not only mourn but also laugh, eat and make music.

teile.einleitung: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart is one of the most famous composers of all time. He was born in Salzburg in 1756 and was a child prodigy at the keyboard when he was still very small. In his short life he wrote more than 600 pieces of music that are still played all over the world today.
wichtigste: Mozart was born in Salzburg on 27 January 1756.
He died in Vienna on 5 December 1791, aged only 35.
At about five years old he was already composing his first little pieces.
As a child he travelled across half of Europe with his family, including through Switzerland.
He wrote operas, symphonies, piano concertos and church music.
His best-known works include The Magic Flute and Eine kleine Nachtmusik.
Mozart is one of the main figures of the Viennese Classical style.

abschnitte.text: Mozart was born in the **Getreidegasse** in Salzburg, which at that time was a prince-archbishopric of its own. His father Leopold was a musician and taught him and his older sister Maria Anna, known as Nannerl. Wolfgang was already playing the keyboard at the age of three. At about five he wrote his first **compositions**.

His father travelled with the two children to many royal courts to show off their talent. The great journey lasted from 1763 to 1766 and went to Munich, Paris and London, among other places. On the way home in 1766, the family also stopped in **Switzerland**, for example in Geneva, Lausanne, Bern and Zurich. Later Mozart travelled to Italy several times, where he learnt a lot about opera.

In 1781 Mozart moved to **Vienna** and worked as a freelance musician. He gave concerts, taught pupils and sold his works. In 1782 he married Constanze Weber. Although he sometimes earned well, he often had money worries.

Mozart wrote more than 600 works, which are numbered in the **Köchel catalogue**. Famous operas are The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and **The Magic Flute** of 1791. Almost everyone knows the serenade Eine kleine Nachtmusik. He was unable to finish his Requiem, a mass for the dead. His pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it after his death.

Together with Joseph Haydn and Ludwig van Beethoven, Mozart belongs to the **Viennese Classical** period. His music often sounds light and cheerful, but it is very skilfully built. In Salzburg you can visit his birthplace, and every summer the Salzburg Festival takes place there. Even a sweet, the Mozartkugel, is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who invents pieces of music and writes them down.
A play in which the performers sing their lines and an orchestra plays.
A large piece of music for orchestra with several parts.
A child who can do something exceptionally well at a very early age.

gewusst: Mozart's baptismal name was Joannes Chrysostomus Wolfgangus Theophilus, and Amadeus is the Latin form of Theophilus.
Even as a child Mozart could play the keyboard with the keys covered, to amaze his audience.
The Mozartkugel was only invented by a Salzburg confectioner about 100 years after Mozart's death.

teile.einleitung: Javier Sotomayor is a former high jumper from Cuba. Since 1993 he has held the men's high jump world record of 2.45 metres. That is higher than many ceilings, and for more than 30 years nobody has beaten this height.
wichtigste: Javier Sotomayor was born in Cuba in 1967.
On 27 July 1993 in Salamanca in Spain he jumped 2.45 metres.
This world record still stands in 2026.
He was the first person to jump over 8 feet, which is 2.44 metres.
In 1992 he became Olympic champion in Barcelona.
He jumped using the Fosbury flop technique, going over the bar backwards.

abschnitte.text: Javier Sotomayor was born on 13 October 1967 in Limonar in Cuba. Even as a teenager he stood out for his enormous jumping power. At only 16 he was already jumping over 2.30 metres. He became one of Cuba's best-known **athletes** and is still a national hero there today.

In 1988 in Salamanca Sotomayor set his first world record with 2.43 metres. A year later in Puerto Rico he became the first person to clear 2.44 metres, which is exactly **8 feet**. On 27 July 1993 in Salamanca he raised the world record to 2.45 metres. He has also held the indoor world record of 2.43 metres since 1989.

At the 1992 Olympic Games in Barcelona, Sotomayor won the gold medal. He was outdoor world champion twice, in Stuttgart in 1993 and in Athens in 1997. At the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney he won silver. However, his career was overshadowed by a **doping ban** after banned substances were found in a test in 1999.

Sotomayor jumped with the **Fosbury flop**, in which you go over the bar backwards and head first. The American Dick Fosbury made this technique famous at the 1968 Olympic Games. Today practically all high jumpers jump this way. What matters is a fast, curved run-up and a powerful take-off from one leg.

abschnitte.titel: Why the record has lasted so long
abschnitte.text: The high jump world record is one of the oldest men's world records in athletics. Many top jumpers today reach about 2.35 to 2.40 metres, but nobody has yet managed 2.45 metres. Mutaz Essa Barshim from Qatar and others narrowly failed at the mark. In women's high jump, Yaroslava Mahuchikh from Ukraine set a new **world record** of 2.10 metres in 2024.

begriffe.erklaerung: The best performance ever officially measured in a sport anywhere in the world.
A high jump technique in which you jump over the bar backwards.
Sports such as running, jumping and throwing.
Banned substances that athletes use to try to improve their performance.

gewusst: Sotomayor jumped about half a metre higher than his own height.
He holds the world record both indoors and outdoors and has held both for more than 30 years.
A normal football goal is only 2.44 metres high, so Sotomayor's record is one centimetre higher.

teile.einleitung: ‘Knights and knaves’ is a famous kind of logic puzzle. On an imaginary island live knights, who always tell the truth, and knaves, who always lie. Only by clever thinking can you work out who is who.
wichtigste: Knights always tell the truth, knaves always lie.
You cannot recognise the people by how they look, only by what they say.
These puzzles were made famous by the American mathematician Raymond Smullyan.
You solve them by trying out both possibilities for each person.
If an assumption leads to a contradiction, it must be false.
Nobody on the island can say the sentence ‘I am a knave’.
Puzzles like these train logical thinking of the kind also needed in mathematics and computer science.

abschnitte.titel: The island of knights and knaves
abschnitte.text: Imagine an island where two kinds of people live. The **knights** always tell the truth, whatever you ask them. The **knaves** always lie: every one of their statements is false. From the outside they all look the same, so you can only tell them apart by what they say. The task is to work out from a few statements who is a knight and who is a knave.

These puzzles became famous through the American mathematician and logician **Raymond Smullyan**, who lived from 1919 to 2017. In his book ‘What Is the Name of This Book?’ from 1978 he presented many such puzzles. Smullyan was not only a professor but also a magician and a pianist. But similar puzzles about liars and truth-tellers have existed for much longer. One well-known example is the puzzle of two guards at two doors, one of whom always lies.

The most important method is called **case analysis**. You assume, for example, that the first person is a knight and check what then follows from all the statements. If everything fits together, that is a possible solution. If you get a **contradiction**, something that would have to be both true and false at the same time, the assumption was wrong. Then the person must be a knave, and you check that case.

A says: ‘B is lying.’ B says: ‘A and C are both lying.’ C says: ‘B is telling the truth.’ Let us assume A is a knight; then B is a knave and his statement is false, which fits, because A is not lying. C claims that B is telling the truth, which is false, so C is also a **knave**, and everything fits together. If, on the other hand, A were a knave, then B would be a knight, and according to B, C would be a liar; but C would be right in his statement about B, which is a contradiction. So only A is telling the truth.

Some sentences cannot be said by anyone on the island. A knight cannot claim ‘I am a knave’, because that would be a lie. A knave cannot say it either, because then it would be true. So if you hear this sentence, something is wrong with the puzzle. Thinking like this belongs to **propositional logic**, which is also important when programming computers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of correct and consistent thinking.
When two statements cannot both be true at the same time.
A method in which you check all the possibilities one after the other.
A sentence that is either true or false.

gewusst: If you ask someone on the island ‘Are you a knight?’, knights and knaves both answer yes, so this question does not help.
With a single clever question you can find out which of two doors leads to freedom, even if you do not know whether the guard is lying.
Raymond Smullyan also wrote puzzle books about chess, in which you have to work out which moves were played earlier.

teile.einleitung: Roger Federer is a tennis player from Basel and one of the most famous sportspeople in Switzerland. He won 20 Grand Slam singles titles and thrilled people all over the world with his elegant game. He ended his career in 2022.
wichtigste: Roger Federer was born in Basel on 8 August 1981.
He won 20 Grand Slam singles titles.
He won Wimbledon eight times, more often than any other man.
He was world number 1 for 237 weeks in a row, a record.
Altogether he won 103 tournaments on the ATP Tour.
In 2014 he won the Davis Cup with Switzerland.
In September 2022 he retired from professional tennis at the Laver Cup in London.

abschnitte.text: Roger Federer grew up in the **Basel** area; his father is Swiss and his mother comes from South Africa. Even as a little boy he played tennis and football. At the Swiss Indoors in Basel he was a **ball boy** as a child. As a teenager he was sometimes very hot-headed and would occasionally throw his racket. At 14 he moved to the National Training Centre in Ecublens on Lake Geneva, where he learnt French.

In 2003 Federer won his first **Grand Slam title** at Wimbledon. Many more followed: 8 at Wimbledon in total, 6 at the Australian Open, 5 at the US Open and 1 at the French Open in 2009. With these 20 titles he held the record for a long time, until Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic overtook him. He was world number 1 for 310 weeks, 237 of them without a break. At his home tournament, the Swiss Indoors in Basel, he won ten times.

At the 2008 **Olympic Games** in Beijing, Federer won gold in the doubles with Stan Wawrinka. In London in 2012 he won silver in the singles. In 2014, together with Wawrinka, he won the **Davis Cup** for Switzerland for the first time, the most important team competition in men's tennis. He was voted Swiss Sportsman of the Year several times. In 2020 Swissmint issued a 20-franc coin with his portrait.

Federer was known for his elegant, almost weightless game. His **forehand** was feared, and many fans admired his one-handed backhand. He played fast and aggressively and liked to come to the net. His movements looked so light that some spectators said he floated across the court. At the same time he was regarded as an especially fair sportsman and won many awards for fair play.

After several knee operations, Federer ended his career at the **Laver Cup** in London in September 2022. In his last match he played doubles with his long-time rival Rafael Nadal, and both cried when he said goodbye. As early as 2003 he set up the **Roger Federer Foundation**. It supports education projects for children in southern Africa and in Switzerland. Federer is married to the former tennis player Mirka and has four children, including two pairs of twins.

begriffe.erklaerung: The four most important tennis tournaments: the Australian Open, the French Open, Wimbledon and the US Open.
A tennis competition in which national teams play against each other.
A list showing which players are currently the best.
A shot in which the back of the hand faces the direction of the shot.

gewusst: Roger Federer was the first living person to appear on a Swiss coin.
As a child Federer was a ball boy at the tournament in Basel that he later won ten times.
In 2008 Federer and Nadal played a Wimbledon final lasting almost five hours, which many consider one of the best matches in the history of tennis.

teile.einleitung: Guillaume-Henri Dufour was a Swiss general, engineer and map-maker. In 1847 he led the federal troops in the Sonderbund War, and he created the first accurate map of the whole of Switzerland. The Dufourspitze, at 4634 metres the highest peak in Switzerland, is named after him.
wichtigste: Dufour lived from 1787 to 1875 and worked mainly in Geneva.
He was an officer, engineer, map-maker and politician.
In the Sonderbund War of 1847 he was general of the federal army.
He conducted the war quickly and with as few victims as possible.
Under his leadership the Dufour Map was made, the first accurate map of the whole of Switzerland.
In 1863 he helped to found the Red Cross.
The Dufourspitze in the Monte Rosa massif has borne his name since 1863.

abschnitte.text: **Guillaume-Henri Dufour** was born in Konstanz in 1787 but grew up in Geneva. He studied at the famous École polytechnique in Paris and became an officer in Napoleon’s army. Later he returned to Switzerland and worked as an engineer in Geneva. There, among other things, he built bridges and quays.

In 1847 the **Sonderbund War** broke out between the Catholic conservative cantons and the majority of the Confederation. The Diet elected Dufour as general. He ordered his soldiers to treat prisoners and the wounded well and to spare the population. The war lasted just under four weeks and cost comparatively few lives; afterwards, in 1848, the modern **federal state** was created.

From 1832 Dufour led the survey of the whole of Switzerland. This produced the **Topographical Map of Switzerland**, which appeared between 1845 and 1865 at a scale of 1 to 100,000. Mountains were shown on it with shading so that they look almost three-dimensional. At the time the **Dufour Map** was one of the best maps in the world.

In 1863, together with Henri Dunant, Dufour belonged to the **Committee of Five** in Geneva, which became the International Committee of the Red Cross. He was the first president of this committee. In 1864 he chaired the conference at which the first Geneva Convention for the protection of wounded soldiers was agreed. His reputation as a general helped the states to take the idea seriously.

In 1863 the Federal Council named the highest peak of the Monte Rosa massif the **Dufourspitze** in his honour. At 4634 metres it is the highest mountain whose summit stands on Swiss soil. In Geneva there is an equestrian statue of Dufour on the Place de Neuve. Dufour is still seen today as a model of a humane and level-headed military leader.

begriffe.erklaerung: The supreme commander of the Swiss army, elected only in wartime or great crises.
A person who draws and produces maps (a cartographer).
A short civil war in Switzerland in 1847.
Shows how much something is reduced on a map.

gewusst: Dufour worked for the white cross on a red background to become the shared emblem of the Swiss troops.
The Dufourspitze used to be called Gornerhorn or Höchste Spitze.
Dufour was elected general several times in his life, not only in 1847.

teile.einleitung: The North Atlantic Treaty is the founding treaty of NATO, a defensive alliance of states from Europe and North America. It was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949. Its most famous part is Article 5: an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
wichtigste: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed by 12 states on 4 April 1949.
It founded NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization.
The treaty is short and has only 14 articles.
Under Article 5 the members help each other if one of them is attacked.
Article 5 has been invoked only once, after the attacks of 11 September 2001.
Since 2024 NATO has had 32 member states.
Switzerland is neutral and not a member, but works with NATO in a partnership.

abschnitte.text: The North Atlantic Treaty is an **alliance treaty** in which states promise to protect each other. It came about after the Second World War, when many Western European countries were afraid of the Soviet Union. On 4 April 1949 twelve founding states signed it in Washington, among them the USA, Canada, Great Britain, France and Italy. This led to **NATO**, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Its headquarters are now in Brussels in Belgium.

The most important part is **Article 5**, the mutual defence clause. It says that an armed attack on one member is regarded as an attack on all members. But each country decides for itself what help it gives, and this can also be support without soldiers. This rule is meant to deter possible attackers, because they would have to deal with the whole alliance. It is often compared with the motto ‘One for all, all for one’.

On 11 September 2001 terrorists in the USA hijacked four planes and flew two of them into the towers of the **World Trade Center** in New York. Almost 3000 people were killed. The very next day NATO declared that the **mutual defence clause** could apply, and at the beginning of October 2001 this was confirmed. It was the first and so far only time that Article 5 has been used. Other members then sent, for example, surveillance planes that monitored the airspace over the USA.

Since 1949 NATO has grown a great deal, especially after the end of the Cold War. Many states from Eastern Europe joined, for example Poland, the Czech Republic and the Baltic states. After Russia's attack on Ukraine in 2022, **Finland** joined in 2023 and **Sweden** in 2024. This brings NATO to 32 states. New members can only be admitted if all existing members agree.

Switzerland is not a NATO member because it has been **neutral** for a long time. This means that it does not take part in other states' wars and does not belong to any military alliance. Since 1996, however, it has taken part in the **Partnership for Peace**. Through it, Switzerland works with NATO on things such as training, disaster relief and peacebuilding. Swiss soldiers help, for example, with an international peace mission in Kosovo.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of states that support each other.
The moment when the members stand by an attacked partner under Article 5.
When a country does not take sides in wars.
Strength that is meant to stop a possible attacker from attacking at all.

gewusst: The whole North Atlantic Treaty is so short that it fits on a few pages.
Iceland is one of NATO's founding members, even though it has no army of its own.
Although NATO was founded as protection against the Soviet Union, it invoked Article 5 for the first time because of a terrorist attack.

teile.einleitung: The Great Depression was the most severe economic crisis of the 20th century. It began in 1929 with a stock market crash in New York and spread to almost the whole world. Millions of people lost their jobs, and its consequences changed politics in many countries.
wichtigste: The trigger was the crash on the New York Stock Exchange in October 1929.
The fall in share prices began on Thursday 24 October 1929.
In Europe people often speak of Black Friday.
Many banks and companies went bankrupt.
In the USA around 1933, about one worker in four was unemployed.
In Germany the crisis contributed to the rise of the Nazis.
Switzerland also suffered badly from the crisis in the 1930s.

abschnitte.text: In the 1920s many people in the USA bought **shares**, often with borrowed money. Prices kept rising, even though the companies were not actually worth that much. On 24 October 1929 prices on the **New York Stock Exchange** on Wall Street suddenly collapsed. The fall continued over the following days. Many people lost all their savings.

One cause was **speculation**, that is betting on prices rising higher and higher. In addition, more goods were being produced than people could buy. When the banks got into difficulty, many people took out their money at the same time. As a result, thousands of banks went bust. Because many countries were linked by loans, the crisis quickly spread to Europe.

Factories closed and millions became **unemployed**. In the USA people queued in long lines outside soup kitchens. In Germany in 1932 about six million people were out of work. Many countries introduced high **customs duties** to protect their own economies. But this made world trade even smaller and the crisis even worse.

The crisis reached Switzerland a little later, but it hit the country hard in the 1930s. The **watch industry** and embroidery in eastern Switzerland in particular lost many customers abroad. Tens of thousands of people lost their jobs. In 1936 Switzerland devalued its franc so that Swiss goods became cheaper abroad.

In the USA, President Franklin D. Roosevelt launched the **New Deal** from 1933, a big programme of building projects and social help. In Germany, Adolf Hitler and the Nazis exploited people's hardship to come to power. From the crisis people learnt that states and central banks should step in during bad times. Today there are, for example, rules that protect savings in banks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A marketplace where shares and other securities are bought and sold.
A small part of a company that you can buy.
People want to work but cannot find a job.
Buying something in the hope of being able to sell it later for more.

gewusst: Because of the time difference, the news of the crash only caused a stir in Europe on the Friday, which is why people here speak of Black Friday.
Only in 1954 did the most important US share index get back to its level before the crash.
The famous photo ‘Migrant Mother’ shows a poor mother with her children during the crisis in the USA.

teile.einleitung: The United Nations, the UN for short, is the largest international organisation in the world. Almost all the states on Earth belong to it: 193 member states (as of 2026). Its most important aim is to keep peace in the world.
wichtigste: The United Nations was founded in 1945 after the Second World War.
It has 193 member states (as of 2026).
Its headquarters are in New York.
Geneva is the UN's second most important location.
Switzerland has been a member since 2002.
The Security Council has five permanent members with a right of veto.
There are six official languages.

abschnitte.text: After the terrible **Second World War**, the states wanted to prevent another war. In June 1945 they signed the **Charter of the United Nations** in San Francisco. It came into force on 24 October 1945, which is why this day is United Nations Day. At the start the UN had 51 members. Its predecessor was the League of Nations, based in Geneva.

In the **General Assembly** each member state has one vote, whether large or small. The **Security Council** has 15 members and deals with peace and security. The USA, Russia, China, Great Britain and France are permanent members and can stop any decision with their veto. The organisation is led by the Secretary-General; since 2017 this has been António Guterres from Portugal, whose term ends at the end of 2026.

The UN sends **blue helmets** to crisis areas to monitor peace. It works for human rights, which were set out in a declaration in 1948. The UN includes many specialised agencies, for example the children's fund UNICEF and the World Health Organization. The World Food Programme helps people who are going hungry.

Switzerland only joined on 10 September 2002, after the people had said yes in a **vote**. In Geneva stands the Palais des Nations, the UN's European headquarters. Thousands of people work there for the United Nations. In 2023 and 2024 Switzerland was a member of the Security Council for the first time.

The six official languages are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. The UN **flag** is light blue with a white map of the world surrounded by olive branches. Olive branches are an ancient symbol of peace. The headquarters in New York is a tall glass tower on the East River.

begriffe.erklaerung: The founding treaty containing the UN's most important rules.
An objection with which a single country can block a decision.
UN soldiers with blue helmets whose job is to keep the peace.
A country that officially belongs to an organisation.

gewusst: The site of the UN headquarters in New York is regarded as international territory.
Switzerland was one of the last countries to join the UN, even though many UN offices had been in Geneva for a long time.
The Vatican is not a member of the UN but has observer status there.

t97zga8.t: International Committee of the Red Cross

teile.einleitung: The International Committee of the Red Cross, or ICRC for short, is an aid organisation based in Geneva. It protects and helps people who suffer in wars and armed conflicts. Hardly any other organisation has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize so often.
wichtigste: The ICRC was founded in Geneva in 1863.
The idea came from the Geneva businessman Henry Dunant.
The ICRC received the Nobel Peace Prize three times, in 1917, 1944 and 1963.
It helps the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war zones.
The ICRC watches over compliance with the Geneva Conventions.
Its emblem, a red cross on a white background, is the Swiss flag reversed.
The ICRC works in a neutral, impartial and independent way.

abschnitte.text: The ICRC is a private, independent organisation under Swiss law. Its governing committee is made up only of Swiss citizens. Its staff, however, work in many countries around the world, often exactly where fighting is going on. The ICRC belongs to the **Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement**, which also includes the national societies such as the Swiss Red Cross.

In 1859 **Henry Dunant** passed by after a bloody battle at Solferino in northern Italy. Thousands of wounded men lay on the battlefield without help. Together with women from the village, Dunant organised emergency care for soldiers on both sides. Later he wrote the book ‘A Memory of Solferino’ about it and called for voluntary relief societies in every country.

In 1863 five citizens of Geneva, among them Henry Dunant, Gustave Moynier and General Guillaume-Henri Dufour, founded the committee. As early as 1864 several states signed the first **Geneva Convention** to protect wounded soldiers. Today the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 are the main ones, and almost every state in the world has recognised them. They form the core of **international humanitarian law**.

The ICRC visits prisoners of war and detainees in conflicts and makes sure they are treated humanely. It brings water, food and medical help to war zones. With its **tracing service** it helps families separated by war to find each other again. It also reminds governments and armies to keep to the rules of war.

The ICRC received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917 for its work in the First World War. In 1944 it was honoured again for its efforts in the Second World War. In 1963, on its 100th anniversary, it received the prize together with the League of Red Cross Societies. Henry Dunant himself received the very first **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1901.

The red cross on a white background was chosen in honour of Switzerland by swapping the colours of the Swiss flag. In countries with a mainly Muslim population the **Red Crescent** is used. In Geneva you can visit the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum. Switzerland is also the depositary state of the Geneva Conventions, which means it keeps the treaties.

begriffe.erklaerung: Not taking any side in a dispute or war.
International treaties that set out how the wounded, prisoners and civilians are protected in war.
Something that serves the well-being and protection of people.
A soldier who is held by the other side during a war.

gewusst: The ICRC is the organisation that has received the Nobel Peace Prize most often.
Besides the cross and the crescent, there has been a third protective emblem since 2005: the Red Crystal.
At the end of his life Henry Dunant was poor and lived a quiet life in Heiden in the canton of Appenzell Ausserrhoden.

teile.einleitung: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was a German physicist who discovered a mysterious kind of radiation in 1895. These rays pass through the body and make bones visible. For his discovery he received the very first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.
wichtigste: Röntgen lived from 1845 to 1923.
He studied in Zurich at what is now ETH.
On 8 November 1895 in Würzburg he discovered a new kind of radiation.
He called them X-rays; in German-speaking countries they are called Röntgen rays.
The first famous X-ray image shows his wife's hand with her wedding ring.
In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
He did not patent his discovery, so that everyone could use it.

abschnitte.text: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was born on 27 March 1845 in Lennep, which today is part of Remscheid in Germany. He grew up partly in the Netherlands. Because he did not have the usual school-leaving certificate, he studied at the **Zurich Polytechnic**, today's ETH. He graduated there in 1868 as a mechanical engineer and then earned his doctorate at the University of Zurich. Later he became a professor in Würzburg and in Munich.

On 8 November 1895 in **Würzburg**, Röntgen was experimenting with a glass tube through which electric current flowed. Although he had covered the tube with black card, a screen nearby lit up. So there had to be an invisible **radiation** that passed through the card. Because he did not know what it was, he called it X-rays.

Röntgen noticed that the rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped by bone and metal. He took a picture of the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha. In the picture you could see the bones of her fingers and her wedding ring. When the discovery became known, the whole world was thrilled. Within just a few months doctors were using the rays to find **broken bones**.

In 1901 the **Nobel Prize** was awarded for the first time, and Röntgen received the prize for physics. He gave the prize money to the University of Würzburg for research. He did not want a patent on his invention, so that everyone could benefit from it. In his honour, chemical element 111 is called **roentgenium**.

Today X-rays are used every day in hospitals and dental surgeries. At the airport they are used to look inside suitcases. In computed tomography, many X-ray images are combined into detailed cross-section pictures of the body. Because the rays are harmful in large amounts, people protect themselves with **lead aprons** and only take pictures that are needed.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that spreads invisibly through space, like light or heat.
The science that studies the laws of nature, for example light, forces and energy.
A right that allows only the inventor to use or sell an invention.
A famous prize for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.

gewusst: Röntgen very much liked to spend his holidays in Pontresina in the Engadine.
As a pupil Röntgen was expelled from school because he would not give away a classmate who had drawn a caricature of a teacher.
In many countries people say X-ray; only in the German-speaking world and a few other countries are the rays named after Röntgen.

teile.einleitung: Paper is a thin material made of pressed plant fibres that we write, print and paint on. It was invented in China about 2000 years ago. Today we come across it everywhere: in exercise books, books, newspapers, packaging and even as tissues.
wichtigste: Paper was invented in China.
The Chinese official Cai Lun, who improved the process around the year 105, is regarded as its inventor.
Paper is made mainly of plant fibres, today mostly from wood.
Paper reached Europe by way of the Arab world.
In 1390 the first paper mill in the German-speaking world was set up in Nuremberg.
A normal A4 sheet measures 21 by 29.7 centimetres.
Waste paper can be recycled several times to make new paper.

abschnitte.text: Paper was invented in **China**. Archaeologists have found remains of paper there that are more than 2000 years old. The court official **Cai Lun** is often regarded as the inventor; around AD 105 he presented the emperor with an improved method of making it. He used tree bark, hemp, old rags and fishing nets. Before that, people in China wrote on strips of bamboo or on expensive silk.

For a long time the Chinese kept the method secret. In the 8th century people in the Arab world also learnt to make paper, for example in **Samarkand** and Baghdad. The knowledge reached Europe via Spain and Italy in the 12th and 13th centuries. In Nuremberg in 1390, **Ulman Stromer** founded one of the first paper mills north of the Alps. Before that, people in Europe mostly wrote on **parchment** made from animal skin, which was very expensive.

In the past paper was made from old rags, which were pounded into a pulp. Today wood is mostly used, from which the fibres are extracted as **wood pulp**. The fibres are mixed with lots of water and spread out on a screen, where they mat together. Then the wet layer is pressed and dried. Large **paper machines** are more than a hundred metres long and produce sheets of paper at high speed.

There are hundreds of kinds of paper, from thin tissue paper to thick cardboard. How heavy a paper is, is given in **grams per square metre**; normal printer paper is usually 80 grams. Formats such as A4 or A5 are standardised: an A4 sheet is exactly half the size of an A3 sheet. Banknotes, tickets, books and packaging are also made of paper. The invention of printing in the 15th century would hardly have been possible without cheap paper.

Making new paper takes a lot of wood, water and energy. That is why **recycling** is important: new paper can be made from waste paper, and this can be done several times. In Switzerland the municipalities collect waste paper and cardboard regularly, usually tied in bundles at the roadside. Recycled paper saves trees and uses less water. At the Basel Paper Mill, a museum in Basel, you can try out for yourself how paper used to be made by hand.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fine fibres obtained from wood, from which paper is made.
A writing material made from treated animal skin, used before paper.
A writing material of the ancient Egyptians, made from the pith of the papyrus plant.
Reusing materials that have been used before in order to make something new.

gewusst: The word ‘paper’ comes from ‘papyrus’, even though papyrus is made differently from paper.
Wasps build their nests out of a kind of paper that they make from chewed wood.
A sheet of paper can only be folded in half about seven or eight times, because it then becomes too thick.

teile.einleitung: Thermal expansion means that almost all substances get bigger when they warm up and smaller when they cool down. That is why the Eiffel Tower is a few centimetres taller in summer than in winter. Engineers always have to take this into account when building bridges, railway tracks and houses.
wichtigste: Most substances expand when warm and contract when cold.
The reason is that the tiniest particles move more strongly when warm.
The iron Eiffel Tower is a few centimetres taller in summer than in winter.
Gases expand much more than solids.
Bridges have expansion joints so that they can expand.
Thermometers work thanks to thermal expansion.
Water is an exception: it expands when it freezes.

abschnitte.text: All substances are made of tiny **particles** that are constantly vibrating. When a substance is heated, the particles vibrate more strongly and need more room. As a result the whole object gets a little bigger. When it cools down, the particles move closer together again. In solids the change is very small; in **gases** it is greatest.

abschnitte.titel: The example of the Eiffel Tower
abschnitte.text: The Eiffel Tower in Paris is about 330 metres high and made of iron. In summer, when the sun heats the metal, it expands. It then becomes a few centimetres taller than on a cold winter's day. On sunny days the top even leans slightly away from the sun, because the side in the sunshine is warmer. Steel gets about a hundredth of a millimetre longer per metre for each degree Celsius.

A long steel bridge can be several decimetres longer in summer than in winter. That is why **expansion joints** are built in, which often look like interlocking teeth. In the past, small gaps were also left between railway rails, which caused the familiar clattering. Power lines sag more in summer than in winter. Without these precautions, rails could buckle or parts could crack.

In a **thermometer**, a liquid expands and rises in a thin tube. A **bimetallic strip** consists of two metal strips that expand by different amounts. It bends when it gets warm and can, for example, switch off an iron or a kettle. A hot-air balloon also flies because warm air expands and so becomes lighter.

Water behaves in a special way: it is densest at 4 degrees Celsius. When it freezes into **ice**, it expands by about 9 per cent. That is why full glass bottles burst in the freezer and water pipes burst in winter. In the Alps, freezing water even splits rocks apart. Because ice is lighter than water, lakes freeze from the top, and the fish survive at the bottom.

begriffe.erklaerung: A deliberate gap in a structure that leaves room for expansion.
A strip made of two different metals that bends when heated.
The tiny building blocks from which all substances are made.
How much mass there is in a certain space, that is how heavy a substance is for its size.

gewusst: The sea also expands when it gets warmer, and this contributes to rising sea levels.
Reinforced concrete holds so well because steel and concrete expand by almost the same amount when heated.
A stuck screw lid on a jar can often be opened if you hold it under warm water.

teile.einleitung: Isaac Newton was an English natural scientist and one of the greatest scientists of all time. In the 17th century he described the law of gravity, also called gravitation. His laws explain why an apple falls from a tree and why the moon circles the Earth.
wichtigste: Isaac Newton lived from 1643 to 1727 in England.
He described the law of gravity, also called the law of gravitation.
He set out three basic laws of motion.
He showed that white light is made up of all the colours of the rainbow.
He built one of the first reflecting telescopes.
His main work, the ‘Principia’, appeared in 1687.
The unit of force is called the newton in his honour.

abschnitte.text: Isaac Newton was born on 4 January 1643 (by today's calendar) in Woolsthorpe in England. His father died before he was born. Newton studied at the University of **Cambridge** and became professor of mathematics there at only 26. Later he ran the Royal Mint in London and was president of the famous Royal Society.

According to legend, a falling apple gave him the idea of **gravitation**. Newton realised that the same force pulls the apple to the ground and keeps the moon in its orbit around the Earth. He described how all bodies attract each other, and do so more strongly the greater their mass and the closer they are. With this he could also calculate the orbits of the planets around the sun.

The first law says: a body stays at rest or keeps moving steadily as long as no force acts on it. This is called **inertia**. The second law describes how a force accelerates a body, and does so less the heavier the body is. The third law states: every force is met by an equal opposing force, just as a rocket pushes gas backwards and so flies forwards.

Using a glass **prism**, Newton split white sunlight into the colours of the rainbow. In this way he proved that white light is a mixture of many colours. To get better images of the sky, he built a **reflecting telescope** in 1668. Telescopes with mirrors like this are still used in astronomy today.

Newton developed a new kind of mathematics, **calculus**, which lets you calculate changes precisely. At almost the same time the German Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz invented the same thing, which led to a long dispute. His book ‘Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica’ of 1687 is regarded as one of the most important works in the history of science. Only Albert Einstein, more than 200 years later, extended Newton's ideas with the theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of attraction between all bodies, which for example makes things fall to the ground.
The property of a body of staying in its state of motion.
A glass block that splits light into its colours.
The unit of force, abbreviated N.

gewusst: During a plague epidemic in 1665 and 1666 the university was closed, and Newton made some of his most important discoveries at home.
In 1705 Newton was knighted by Queen Anne and was allowed to call himself Sir Isaac Newton.
He was buried in the famous Westminster Abbey in London.

teile.einleitung: Machu Picchu is an ancient ruined city of the Incas high in the Andes of Peru. It lies on a mountain ridge above a deep valley and is surrounded by steep peaks. Today Machu Picchu is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most famous sights in the world.
wichtigste: Machu Picchu is in Peru in South America.
The city was built by the Incas in the 15th century.
It lies at about 2430 metres above sea level.
The Spanish did not discover the city during their conquest.
In 1911 the American Hiram Bingham made it known around the world.
Machu Picchu has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
In the Quechua language the name means roughly ‘old mountain’.

abschnitte.text: Machu Picchu lies in the **Andes** in southern Peru, about 75 kilometres north-west of the city of Cusco. The ruins are on a mountain saddle at a height of about 2430 metres. Far below flows the **Urubamba** river. Behind the city rises the pointed mountain Huayna Picchu.

The Incas built Machu Picchu around the middle of the 15th century, probably for their ruler **Pachacuti**. It was probably a royal estate and a religious site. Only about a hundred years later the city was abandoned, at roughly the time of the Spanish conquest. Because the Spanish did not find it, it remained well preserved.

The Incas were masters of building with stone. Many walls are made of stone blocks cut so precisely that they hold together without mortar. On the slopes they laid out **terraces** on which they grew maize and potatoes. The Temple of the Sun and the ritual stone **Intihuatana** are also well known.

Local farmers had known about the ruins for a long time. In 1911 they led the American explorer **Hiram Bingham** there. He had photos of it published in magazines, which made Machu Picchu world-famous. In 1983 UNESCO added the site to its list of **World Heritage** sites.

Every year hundreds of thousands of visitors come from all over the world. You can reach Machu Picchu by train and bus or on foot along the famous **Inca Trail**. To protect the ruins, the number of visitors per day is limited. Llamas often graze on the meadows between the old walls.

begriffe.erklaerung: A people who ruled a large empire in South America in the 15th and 16th centuries.
A long mountain range along the western side of South America.
A step on a slope on which fields are laid out.
The language of the Incas, which is still spoken in Peru today.

gewusst: The Incas had no writing in the usual sense; they used knotted cords called quipus.
In 2007 Machu Picchu was voted one of the ‘New Seven Wonders of the World’.
The Inca walls survived many earthquakes because the stones fit together so precisely.

teile.einleitung: Data ethics asks how to deal properly and fairly with data about people. Mobile phones, apps and websites collect huge amounts of information every day, and laws and principles are meant to protect people while this happens.
wichtigste: The revised Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since 1 September 2023.
In Switzerland the **FDPIC** watches over data protection.
The EU's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) has applied since 25 May 2018.
Data minimisation means collecting only as much data as necessary.
Privacy by design builds data protection into technology from the start.
The Cambridge Analytica scandal of 2018 showed the political power of data.

abschnitte.text: **Personal data** is any information that belongs to a particular person: name, address, photos, location or what someone clicks on online. Data ethics asks who may collect such data, for what purpose and for how long. An important idea is **informational self-determination**. Each person should in principle be able to decide for themselves what happens to their data. Germany's Federal Constitutional Court established this right in 1983 in the **census judgment**.

Since **1 September 2023** Switzerland has had a completely revised **Data Protection Act (DSG)**. It adapts the law to the digital world and to European standards. It protects the data of natural persons, that is of human beings. Compliance is monitored by the **Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC)**. He can open investigations and issue binding orders. The cantons have their own data protection commissioners for cantonal authorities.

The European Union's **General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)** was adopted in 2016 and has applied since **25 May 2018**. It also affects Swiss companies if they offer goods or services to people in the EU. In 2014, in the ‘Google Spain’ case, the European Court of Justice ruled on the **right to be forgotten**.
