A hook-and-loop fastener consists of a **hook strip** and a fluffy strip with many soft loops. When you press the two together, thousands of hooks catch in the loops. If you pull hard, the hooks bend open and let go without breaking. That is why you can open and close the fastener again and again.

It took years for de Mestral to find a suitable material, because cotton was too soft. Only with the plastic **nylon** did he manage to make durable hooks. In 1951 he applied for a patent for the invention in Switzerland and founded the company Velcro. After that, the hook-and-loop fastener spread around the world.

When people transfer ideas from nature to technology, this is called **bionics**. The hook-and-loop fastener is one of the best-known examples. The space agency NASA used it so that objects would not float away in weightlessness. Today it holds together shoes, blood pressure cuffs, cables and much more.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology that copies solutions from nature.
A legal right that secures an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
A tear-resistant plastic from which fibres and fabrics are made.
A plant with round fruits full of tiny hooks.

gewusst: Many people simply say ‘Velcro’ when they mean a hook-and-loop fastener, even though it is a brand name.
Very strong hook-and-loop fasteners can hold objects weighing many kilograms.
When it was introduced, some fashion experts thought the hook-and-loop fastener was too ugly for nice clothes.

teile.einleitung: Separation of powers means that the power in a state is divided between several bodies that are independent of each other. Making laws, carrying them out and judging cases are in different hands. This is meant to stop anyone getting too much power and to keep people’s freedom safe.
wichtigste: State power is divided into three parts: the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.
The legislature passes the laws; in Switzerland this is the Federal Assembly.
The executive carries out the laws; in Switzerland this is the Federal Council.
The judiciary judges cases; at its head is the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne.
The philosopher Montesquieu described this idea in 1748 in his book “The Spirit of the Laws”.
The separation of powers is a pillar of every democracy.
Cantons and municipalities also have a separation of powers.

abschnitte.text: If a single person has all the power, they can make laws as they please and punish people unfairly. The **separation of powers** prevents this by dividing state power. The three powers keep a check on each other, as in a game in which nobody may be player and referee at the same time. This system is also called checks and balances.

The French philosopher **Montesquieu** lived from 1689 to 1755. In his work “The Spirit of the Laws” of 1748 he described how freedom is only possible if the powers are separated. Before him the Englishman John Locke had had similar ideas. These ideas influenced the US Constitution of 1787 and the French Revolution.

The **legislature** is the law-making power, in other words the parliament. The **executive** is the power that carries out the laws, in other words the government and the administration. The **judiciary** is the judicial power, in other words the courts. Each power has its own tasks and may not simply interfere in the work of the others.

At federal level the legislature consists of the **Federal Assembly**, with the National Council of 200 members and the Council of States of 46 members. The executive is the **Federal Council** with seven members. The judiciary is headed by the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne, along with other federal courts in Bellinzona and St Gallen. In the cantons the powers have names such as cantonal council or Grand Council, cantonal government and High Court.

In Switzerland the **people** also have a lot of power, because they can vote on laws and changes to the constitution. Dividing power between the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities is also a way of spreading power. Free media are often called the “fourth estate”, because they keep a critical eye on politics and the authorities. In Switzerland nobody may be a member of the Federal Council and a federal judge at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power, in other words the parliament.
The power that carries out the laws, in other words the government and administration.
The judicial power, in other words the courts.
The most important law of a state, which lays down the basic rules.
A form of state in which the people hold the power.

gewusst: In a dictatorship there is no real separation of powers, because one person or group seizes all the power.
A few years after it appeared, Montesquieu’s book was put on the Catholic Church’s list of banned books.
In Switzerland the Federal Assembly elects both the members of the Federal Council and the federal judges.

teile.einleitung: Plants are living things that make their own food with the help of sunlight. They include huge trees, colourful flowers, grasses, ferns and mosses. Without plants there would be neither enough oxygen to breathe nor food for people and animals.
wichtigste: To grow, plants need above all water, light and air.
Using sunlight, they make sugar in photosynthesis and give off oxygen.
The root is usually in the soil and takes up water and nutrients.
Many plants are made up of root, stem, leaves and flowers.
There are hundreds of thousands of plant species around the world.
The edelweiss is a well-known symbol of the Alps.
Conifers such as the fir stay green even in winter.

abschnitte.text: Most plants we know have a **root**, a stem or trunk, leaves and often flowers. The root is in the soil, holds the plant in place and sucks up water with nutrients. The water is carried through the stem up to the leaves. In the leaves, food is made using light. After pollination, the **flowers** produce fruits and seeds, from which new plants grow.

Plants can make their own food, and this is what makes them different from animals. To do this they need water, **light** and carbon dioxide from the air. The green leaves contain the pigment **chlorophyll**, which captures sunlight. With it the plants build up sugar, and oxygen is produced as waste. This process is called photosynthesis, and it supplies almost all living things on Earth with food and air to breathe.

The plant kingdom includes very different groups: mosses, ferns, conifers and flowering plants. The cactus grows in dry areas such as deserts and stores water in its thick stem; its **spines** are modified leaves. The oak is a mighty broadleaf tree on which **acorns** grow in autumn. The fir belongs to the conifers and keeps its needles in winter, which is why it stays green. Among the largest living things on Earth are the sequoias in California, which grow more than 80 metres tall.

Thousands of different plant species grow in Switzerland, from Ticino to the high Alps. Forest covers about a third of the country's area; common trees are spruce, beech and fir. The **edelweiss**, with its white, felty, star-shaped flowers, is a well-known symbol of the Alps. Other typical alpine flowers are the gentian and the alpine rose. Many rare plants are protected and must not be picked.

Almost everything we eat comes directly or indirectly from plants: cereals, vegetables, fruit and also the feed for farm animals. People also get wood, cotton, paper and many **medicines** from plants. In the mountains, forests protect against avalanches and falling rocks. Plants store carbon and are therefore important for the climate. They also give countless animals food and shelter.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process in which plants use light to make sugar and oxygen from water and carbon dioxide.
The green pigment in leaves that captures sunlight.
When pollen reaches another flower, for example carried by bees or the wind.
A small package containing a plant embryo, from which a new plant grows.

gewusst: Plants grow towards the light, which is why houseplants on a windowsill gradually turn towards the window.
Some plants, such as the sundew, catch small insects to get extra nutrients.
Bamboo is one of the fastest-growing plants and can grow several dozen centimetres in a day.

teile.einleitung: Angel Falls (Salto Ángel) is the highest waterfall on Earth. In Venezuela in South America it plunges about 979 metres. That is more than three times the height of the Eiffel Tower!
wichtigste: Angel Falls is in the south of Venezuela.
With a total height of about 979 metres, it is the highest waterfall in the world.
The longest free fall of the water measures about 807 metres.
The water plunges down from the table mountain Auyán-tepui.
The waterfall lies in Canaima National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
It is named after the American pilot Jimmie Angel.
The local Pemón people call it Kerepakupai Merú.

abschnitte.text: Angel Falls is in the state of Bolívar in south-eastern **Venezuela**. It lies in the middle of the rainforest, far from roads and towns. Visitors usually arrive in the village of Canaima by small plane. From there it is several hours by boat along rivers, followed by a walk.

The water falls from a huge **table mountain**, the Auyán-tepui. Table mountains have steep rock walls and an almost flat plateau on top, like a table. The Auyán-tepui is more than 2000 metres high, and its top is larger than some Swiss cantons. It rains a lot up there, and this water collects and plunges over the edge.

abschnitte.titel: A fall from a giant height
abschnitte.text: Altogether the water falls about 979 metres. The longest uninterrupted part, the **free fall**, measures about 807 metres. Because the height is so great, some of the water turns into fine spray before it reaches the bottom. In the dry season the waterfall carries much less water than in the rainy season.

The local **Pemón** people had known about the waterfall for a long time. The rest of the world learnt of it after the American pilot Jimmie Angel flew over it in 1933. In 1937 Angel landed his plane on top of the table mountain, and the plane got stuck in a bog. Angel and his companions had to walk down to the valley for eleven days.

Angel Falls lies in **Canaima National Park**, one of the largest national parks in South America. Since 1994 the park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On the table mountains live plants and animals that exist nowhere else in the world. They developed up there for a long time, cut off from the lowlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where a river plunges over a rock edge.
A mountain with steep sides and a flat area on top, like a table.
A large natural area that is specially protected.
A list of places that are especially valuable for all of humanity.

gewusst: Angel Falls is about 40 times as high as the drop of the Rhine Falls near Schaffhausen.
Decades later, Jimmie Angel's plane was brought down from the table mountain and now stands outside the airport of Ciudad Bolívar.
Some of the water does not arrive at the bottom as a stream at all, but as mist.

teile.einleitung: A leap year is a year with 366 days instead of 365. The extra day is 29 February. It makes sure that our calendar does not slowly get out of step with the seasons.
wichtigste: A leap year has 366 days; the extra day is 29 February.
The Earth takes about 365 days and just under 6 hours to go once round the sun.
The basic rule: years that can be divided by 4 are leap years.
Century years such as 1900 are not leap years unless they can be divided by 400.
That is why 1900 was not a leap year, but 2000 was.
These rules come from the Gregorian calendar of 1582.
The next leap year after 2024 is 2028.

abschnitte.text: The Earth takes about 365.2422 days to go once round the sun. So this **solar year** is about a quarter of a day longer than 365 days. Without a correction, the calendar would fall behind by just under 6 hours every year. After about 120 years the start of spring would be a whole month out.

A year is a **leap year** if it can be divided by 4, for example 2024 or 2028. But if it can be divided by 100, it is not a leap year, like 1700, 1800 and 1900. If it can also be divided by 400, it is a leap year after all. That is why the year 2000 was a leap year, but the year 2100 will not be.

In 45 BC the Roman general Julius Caesar introduced the **Julian calendar**. In it, simply every fourth year was a leap year. But that was slightly too much, and over the centuries the calendar drifted by about 10 days. In 1582 Pope Gregory XIII had the **Gregorian calendar** introduced, skipping 10 days in the process.

Not all countries switched to the new calendar straight away. In Switzerland the Catholic cantons adopted it first, the Reformed ones only around the year 1700. Some municipalities in the Grisons did not switch until the beginning of the 19th century. So for a time, neighbouring places had different dates.

If you were born on **29 February**, you only have a birthday on the right date every four years. In the other years many people celebrate on 28 February or 1 March. In a leap year, every date after February falls on a day of the week two days later than in the previous year. Some sporting events, such as the Summer Olympic Games, usually take place in leap years.

begriffe.erklaerung: The extra day in a leap year, 29 February.
The time the Earth takes to go once round the sun.
The calendar we use today, introduced in 1582.
A number is divisible when nothing is left over after dividing.

gewusst: In many Catholic countries, Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed directly by Friday 15 October.
Even the Gregorian calendar is not perfect, but it is only one day out after about 3000 years.
The year 2000 was a very rare leap year, because it can be divided by 400.

teile.einleitung: The rule of three is a method of calculation with which you work out a fourth, unknown number from three known numbers. You solve it in three steps, which is where the name comes from. With the rule of three you can work out prices, recipes, working times and much more.
wichtigste: With the rule of three you calculate a fourth value from three known values.
You work in three steps, via the unit, that is via the value for one.
In direct proportion: the more of one, the more of the other.
In inverse proportion: the more of one, the less of the other.
If 3 painters need 12 days, then 4 painters working at the same speed need 9 days.
The rule of three is one of the most important tools in everyday arithmetic.

abschnitte.titel: What is the rule of three?
abschnitte.text: In the rule of three you know a relationship between two quantities, for example amount and price. From it you want to calculate a new value. You always go via the **unit**, that is the value for one item, one person or one day. The three steps are: the starting statement, working out the value for one, and working out the amount you are looking for.

In the **directly proportional** rule of three, one quantity grows with the other. If 3 apples cost 1.50 francs, one apple costs 50 centimes. Then 7 apples cost 7 times 50 centimes, which is 3.50 francs. You divide in the second step and multiply in the third.

In the **inversely proportional** rule of three, one quantity gets smaller when the other gets bigger. If 3 painters need 12 days for a job, a single painter would need three times as long, so 36 days. Four painters can do it in 36 divided by 4, so in 9 days. Here you multiply first and then divide.

A recipe for 4 people needs 200 grams of flour; for 6 people you work out 50 grams per person and get 300 grams. You also use the rule of three to work out fuel consumption, hourly wages or **exchange rates**. If you are quick at mental arithmetic, you can tell in the shop which pack is cheaper per kilo. To do this you compare the **unit price**, that is the price per kilo or litre.

The rule of three only works if the quantities really are evenly connected. A child who is 1.20 metres tall at 6 is not 2.40 metres tall at 12. And if an orchestra plays a song in 5 minutes, an orchestra twice the size does not play it in 2.5 minutes. That is why you should always check whether the result makes sense.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two quantities grow in the same ratio: the more of one, the more of the other.
If one quantity doubles, the other halves.
The value for a single item, one person or one day.
The price for one kilogram, one litre or one item of a product.

gewusst: Merchants in the Middle Ages already used the rule of three and sometimes called it the golden rule because it was so useful.
In Switzerland and Germany it is called Dreisatz, in Austria often Schlussrechnung.
Many questions in entrance exams and aptitude tests can be solved with the rule of three.

teile.einleitung: The Maastricht Treaty is the birth certificate of the European Union. It was signed in 1992 in the Dutch city of Maastricht. It also began the path to a shared currency, the euro.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed in Maastricht on 7 February 1992.
It founded the European Union.
It came into force on 1 November 1993.
Twelve states signed it at the time.
The treaty laid the foundations for the euro.
It introduced citizenship of the Union.
Switzerland is not a member of the EU.

abschnitte.text: Before the treaty there were already the **European Communities**, which worked together mainly on the economy. Maastricht turned them into the **European Union**. The states no longer wanted to cooperate only on trade, but also on foreign policy and on justice and policing. People spoke of three pillars on which the EU stands.

Maastricht lies in the south of the Netherlands on the River Maas, near the borders with Belgium and Germany. There, in December 1991, the heads of government met and reached agreement. The treaty was signed on 7 February 1992. Because every country had to approve it, it only came into force on 1 November 1993.

The treaty decided on a joint **economic and monetary union**. Countries that wanted the euro had to meet strict rules, the **Maastricht criteria**. For example, a state was not supposed to take on new debts of more than 3 per cent of its economic output per year. In 1999 the euro was introduced as electronic money, and in 2002 the coins and notes followed.

Not everyone was enthusiastic. In Denmark the people at first rejected the treaty in a **referendum** in 1992. Only after special rules for Denmark did they say yes in 1993. In France, too, the yes vote was very narrow.

In the same year, on 6 December 1992, Swiss voters rejected joining the **European Economic Area**. Since then Switzerland has governed its relationship with the EU through bilateral agreements. The EU is Switzerland's most important trading partner. The Maastricht Treaty was later revised several times, most recently by the Treaty of Lisbon, which came into force in 2009.

begriffe.erklaerung: A union of many European countries that work closely together.
Several countries use the same money together.
All citizens of an EU country are also citizens of the EU and may, for example, live in other EU countries.
A written agreement that everyone involved must keep to.

gewusst: Since Maastricht the EU has grown from 12 to 27 member states today (as of 2026).
Maastricht is one of the oldest towns in the Netherlands and was already settled in Roman times.
The EU was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2012.

teile.einleitung: Cleopatra VII was the last queen of ancient Egypt before the country became Roman. She lived from 69 to 30 BC and was known for her cleverness and political skill. Amazingly, she lived closer in time to the moon landing in 1969 than to the building of the great pyramids.
wichtigste: Cleopatra VII lived from 69 to 30 BC.
She belonged to the Ptolemaic family, which originally came from Macedonia.
She ruled Egypt from the capital, Alexandria.
She was linked to the Roman Julius Caesar and later to Mark Antony.
After the defeat at Actium in 31 BC she took her own life.
After that, Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire.
In her time the Pyramid of Khufu was already about 2500 years old.

abschnitte.text: Cleopatra VII was a ruler from the **Ptolemaic** dynasty, which had ruled Egypt since Alexander the Great. Her family spoke Greek and was of Macedonian origin. Cleopatra is said to have been the first in her family to learn Egyptian as well, and she spoke several languages. In 51 BC, at the age of 18, she became queen, at first together with her younger brother.

abschnitte.titel: Closer in time to the moon
abschnitte.text: The great pyramids of Giza were built around 2500 BC. So about 2500 years lie between their construction and Cleopatra. Between Cleopatra's death and the **moon landing** in 1969, on the other hand, there are only just under 2000 years. This shows how incredibly long the history of **ancient Egypt** is.

In her quarrel with her brother over the throne, Cleopatra sought help from the powerful Roman **Julius Caesar**. With him she had a son called Caesarion. After Caesar's murder in 44 BC she allied herself with the general **Mark Antony**, with whom she had three children. Together they wanted to build a great empire in the east.

Antony and Cleopatra came into conflict with Octavian, who later became the Emperor Augustus. They were defeated in the sea battle of **Actium** in 31 BC. A year later both took their own lives in Alexandria. According to legend, Cleopatra let a poisonous snake bite her, but this is not reliably proven.

After her death Egypt became a **Roman province**, and the age of the pharaohs was over. Roman writers often portrayed Cleopatra badly because she was an enemy of Rome. Later, plays, for example by William Shakespeare, and Hollywood films made her world-famous. Nobody knows exactly what she looked like; coins show her with a striking nose.

begriffe.erklaerung: The title of the kings and queens of ancient Egypt.
A ruling family that reigns over several generations.
A Greek-Macedonian royal family that ruled Egypt for about 300 years.
An area governed by a larger empire.

gewusst: Cleopatra also lived closer in time to us than to the building of the Pyramid of Khufu.
Her son Caesarion was briefly the last pharaoh after her, but was soon killed by Octavian.
Cleopatra VII is called that because there had already been six queens named Cleopatra in her family before her.

teile.einleitung: Women’s suffrage is the right of women to have a say in elections and votes. In Switzerland women have only been able to vote and stand in elections at federal level since 1971. This made Switzerland one of the last countries in Europe to introduce this right.
wichtigste: On 7 February 1971 Swiss men voted yes at the ballot box to women’s suffrage at federal level.
A first vote in 1959 had still been clearly rejected.
The cantons of Vaud and Neuchâtel were the first cantons to introduce women’s suffrage, in 1959.
Appenzell Ausserrhoden followed only in 1989, at the Landsgemeinde.
Appenzell Innerrhoden had to be forced to do so in 1990 by a ruling of the Federal Supreme Court.
In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp became the first woman elected to the Federal Council.
Today women and men in Switzerland have the same political rights.

abschnitte.titel: What is the right to vote?
abschnitte.text: The **right to vote** allows you to say yes or no in popular votes. The **right to stand for election** allows you to elect politicians or be elected yourself. In Switzerland this is especially important, because the people vote on issues several times a year. For a long time, however, only men aged 20 and over were allowed to have a say; half the population was left out.

Women’s associations were already demanding the vote in the 19th century. Many other countries were faster: New Zealand introduced it in 1893, Germany and Austria in 1918. In Switzerland the men had to vote on it themselves, because a change to the constitution needs a **popular vote**. In 1959 around two thirds of the men rejected women’s suffrage.

On 7 February 1971 the voters accepted women’s suffrage with around 66 per cent saying yes. That same year the first women were elected to the **National Council**. Women could now also have a say in many cantons and municipalities. For many women it was a day of great joy that they had waited decades for.

In the two Appenzells, people vote by raising their hands in the open air at the **Landsgemeinde**. Appenzell Ausserrhoden introduced women’s suffrage in 1989. In Appenzell Innerrhoden the men rejected it once again in 1990. Women then took the case to the **Federal Supreme Court**, which decided on 27 November 1990 that women in Innerrhoden could vote too.

In 1981 the principle of equality between women and men was added to the Federal Constitution. On 14 June 1991 hundreds of thousands of women stopped work in the first big **women’s strike**. Today many women sit in parliament, in governments and on the Federal Council. Even so, people still discuss how real equality can be achieved in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to help decide in popular votes.
The right to elect people to an office or to be elected yourself.
An open-air assembly at which voters decide by raising their hands.
The highest court in Switzerland, based in Lausanne.
Women and men have the same rights and opportunities.

gewusst: Because only men could vote in 1971, men had to decide whether women could have a say.
Appenzell Innerrhoden was the last canton in Switzerland in which women got the vote.
At the Landsgemeinde in Appenzell, a sidearm or the voting card still counts as the sign that someone is entitled to vote.

teile.einleitung: The Helvetic Republic was the name of the Swiss state from 1798 to 1803. It came into being after French troops had invaded the Old Swiss Confederacy. For the first time, Switzerland was a unified state with equal rights for all citizens.
wichtigste: The Helvetic Republic was proclaimed in Aarau on 12 April 1798.
Before that, French troops had defeated the Old Swiss Confederacy.
Switzerland became a unitary state on the French model.
The subject territories were freed and all citizens were equal before the law.
Many people rejected the new state, and there were uprisings.
In 1803 Napoleon ended the Helvetic Republic with the Act of Mediation.
Many ideas from that time can still be found in today's Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: Before 1798, Switzerland consisted of 13 **cantons** that were only loosely linked. In many cantons a few rich families ruled, and areas such as Vaud, Aargau, Thurgau or Ticino were **subject territories** without rights of their own. After the French Revolution of 1789, the wish for freedom and equality grew in Switzerland too. Revolutionaries such as Peter Ochs from Basel and Frédéric-César de La Harpe from Vaud sought help in France.

At the beginning of 1798, French troops marched into Switzerland. On 5 March 1798 Bern was captured after the battle at Grauholz, and the Old Swiss Confederacy collapsed. The French took the Bernese state treasury back to France. On 12 April 1798 the **Helvetic Republic** was proclaimed in Aarau.

The republic was a **unitary state** in which the cantons were merely administrative districts. It was governed by a Directory with five members and a parliament. The capital was first Aarau, then Lucerne and later Bern. All citizens were now equal before the law, torture was abolished, and there was freedom of the press and freedom to settle anywhere.

In Central Switzerland in particular, many people fought against the new order. In September 1798 French troops brutally crushed an uprising in Nidwalden. In 1799 Switzerland became a battlefield between France, Austria and Russia, and the Russian general Suvorov led his army over the Alpine passes. Hunger, poverty and quarrels between supporters and opponents of the republic weakened the state badly.

In 1803 **Napoleon** issued the **Act of Mediation**, which made Switzerland a league of cantons again. New cantons were created, such as Aargau, Thurgau, Vaud, Ticino, St Gallen and the Grisons. The Helvetic Republic also introduced the **franc** as the Swiss currency. Ideas such as equal rights for all citizens lived on and shaped the modern federal state in 1848.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without a king, in which the people or elected representatives govern.
A state that is run centrally by one government, without strong member states.
An area that was ruled by other cantons and had no rights of its own.
The constitution that Napoleon gave Switzerland in 1803.

gewusst: In 1799 the educator Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi cared for orphans in Stans whose parents had died in the uprising in Nidwalden.
An uprising against the Helvetic government in 1802 is called the ‘Stecklikrieg’ (stick war), because many fighters were armed only with clubs.
During the Helvetic Republic there was a Swiss ministry of education for the first time, led by Philipp Albert Stapfer.

teile.einleitung: Johanna Spyri was a Swiss writer from the canton of Zurich. She wrote the story of ‘Heidi’, the girl who lives with her grandfather on an alpine pasture. Today Heidi is one of the best-known children's books in the world.
wichtigste: Johanna Spyri was born in Hirzel in the canton of Zurich in 1827.
She died in Zurich in 1901.
Her most famous work is ‘Heidi’, published in two parts in 1880 and 1881.
Heidi has been translated into a great many languages.
The story is set in the mountains of the Grisons near Maienfeld and in Frankfurt.
Heidi has inspired many films and a famous Japanese cartoon series.
Besides Heidi, Spyri wrote many other stories for children and adults.

abschnitte.text: Johanna Spyri was born Johanna Louise Heusser in **Hirzel** on 12 June 1827. Her father was a doctor, and her mother, Meta Heusser-Schweizer, wrote poems and hymns. Johanna grew up with many brothers and sisters in a village above Lake Zurich. The rural surroundings later shaped her stories.

In 1852 she married the lawyer Johann Bernhard Spyri, who later became town clerk of Zurich. The couple had a son, Bernhard, who died young of an illness in 1884. Her husband died in the same year. Johanna Spyri only began writing when she was over 40 and became a successful **writer**.

The orphan **Heidi** is taken to her grumpy grandfather, the Alm-Öhi (Alm Uncle), on an alpine pasture above Maienfeld. There she makes friends with Peter the goatherd and loves life in the mountains. Then Heidi has to go to Frankfurt to stay with Clara, a girl in a wheelchair, and becomes very **homesick**. Back on the mountain, Clara visits Heidi and learns to walk again there.

Heidi is one of the most translated books in Swiss literature. There are many film versions, for example a Swiss cinema film from 2015 with Bruno Ganz as the Alm-Öhi. Especially well known is the Japanese **cartoon series** of 1974, which the future animation master Hayao Miyazaki also worked on. Thanks to this series, Heidi is particularly popular in Japan.

To this day Heidi shapes the image of Switzerland abroad, with mountains, alpine pastures, goats and cheese. Near **Maienfeld** in the Grisons there is a Heidi village that many tourists visit every year. In Hirzel a museum remembers Johanna Spyri. Her grave is in the Sihlfeld cemetery in Zurich.

begriffe.erklaerung: A person who writes books and stories.
Heidi's grandfather, who lives alone on the alpine pasture.
A sad longing for home.
A text that has been carried over from one language into another.

gewusst: The first Heidi volume appeared in 1880 without Johanna Spyri's full name on the book.
Because of the story, the area around Maienfeld is now advertised to tourists as ‘Heidiland’.
Johanna Spyri only began publishing stories when she was over 40.

teile.einleitung: The Taj Mahal is a magnificent tomb of white marble in the city of Agra in India. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan had it built for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal. It is regarded as one of the most beautiful buildings in the world and as a monument to love.
wichtigste: The Taj Mahal stands in Agra in northern India on the River Yamuna.
Shah Jahan had it built as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631 giving birth to her 14th child.
Construction lasted from about 1632 to 1648; the whole complex was only finished a few years later.
It is built of white marble and decorated with precious stones.
It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
Millions of people visit it every year.

abschnitte.text: **Shah Jahan** was a ruler of the Mughal Empire, which ruled large parts of India. He loved his wife **Mumtaz Mahal** very much; she even went with him on military campaigns. In 1631 she died giving birth to her 14th child. In his grief, Shah Jahan had the most magnificent tomb that had ever existed built for her.

About 20,000 workers, stonemasons and artists worked on the Taj Mahal. The white **marble** was brought from Makrana, several hundred kilometres away. Elephants helped to transport heavy loads. The main building was finished around 1648, and the gardens and outbuildings a few years later.

The tomb stands on a large platform with four slender **minarets** at the corners. In the middle rises a huge dome, which is more than 70 metres high including its tip. The walls are decorated with writing from the Qur'an and flower patterns made of inlaid precious stones. In front of the building lies a large garden with a long pool of water in which the Taj Mahal is reflected.

Inside are the **cenotaphs**, that is decorative tombs, of Mumtaz Mahal and Shah Jahan. The real graves lie below them in a chamber. In his last years Shah Jahan was held prisoner by his son. After his death in 1666 he was buried next to his wife.

The Taj Mahal is India's best-known building and a symbol of the country. It has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1983. In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in a worldwide poll. Because exhaust fumes discolour the marble, ordinary cars are not allowed to drive near it.

begriffe.erklaerung: A building over or for a grave, in memory of someone who has died.
The title of the rulers of the Mughal Empire in India.
A slender tower belonging to a mosque or an Islamic building.
A hard, often white stone that can be polished beautifully.

gewusst: Depending on the daylight, the white marble shimmers pink, golden or almost silver.
The four minarets lean slightly outwards so that they would not fall onto the dome in an earthquake.
Taj Mahal means roughly ‘crown of the palace’.

teile.einleitung: Logic puzzles are brain teasers that you solve not with knowledge but with careful thinking. Often the answer seems obvious at first glance, but it is wrong. If you think it through step by step, you will find the trick.
wichtigste: You solve logic puzzles by careful thinking rather than guessing.
Many puzzles tempt you with a quick but wrong answer.
An exercise book and a pen for 1.10 francs: the pen costs 5 centimes, not 10.
Five machines take as long for five parts as 100 machines for 100 parts, namely 5 minutes.
With water lilies that double every day, the pond is half covered on the day before the end.
All 12 months have at least 28 days.
Drawings, tables and equations help you solve puzzles.

abschnitte.text: A logic puzzle is a task in which you draw a certain conclusion from the information given. You do not need any special knowledge for it, but **logical thinking**. Some puzzles are maths problems, others are about orders, days of the week or truth and lies. **Sudoku** and picture puzzles are also well-known forms.

abschnitte.titel: The trap of the quick answer
abschnitte.text: If an exercise book and a pen together cost 1.10 francs and the exercise book costs 1 franc more, many people immediately think the pen costs 10 centimes. But then the exercise book would cost 1.10 francs and everything together 1.20 francs. The right answer is: the pen costs **5 centimes** and the exercise book 1.05 francs. With water lilies that double every day, the pond is half covered after 29 days, not after 15.

A father is 36 and his son is 12. In 12 years the father will be 48 and the son 24, so then the father will be exactly twice as old. If a train leaves at 14:45 and travels for 1 hour and 50 minutes, it arrives at 16:35. If today is Wednesday, in 10 days it will be **Saturday**, because after 7 days it is Wednesday again. If five children each greet each other once, there are **10 handshakes**.

If Anna is taller than Ben, Carla is shorter than Ben and Dario is taller than Anna, you get a row: Dario, Anna, Ben, Carla. So **Carla** is the shortest. With red and blue socks in a drawer, 3 socks are enough to be sure of having two of the same colour. This is called the **pigeonhole principle**: with only two colours, the third sock must match one of the first two.

A very old puzzle is the one about the farmer who has to take a **wolf, a goat and a cabbage** across a river in a small boat. Puzzles with knights, who always tell the truth, and knaves, who always lie, are also popular. The so-called Einstein puzzle asks you to work out from many clues who owns a zebra. Tasks like these train careful reading and putting things together.

Read the task slowly and carefully: the trick is often hidden in a single word. Check your answer by putting it back into the task. Draw sketches or make a **table** if there are many people or things involved. And if a solution seems too easy, it is worth taking a second look.

begriffe.erklaerung: The study of correct reasoning.
If you put more things into compartments than there are compartments, at least two end up in one compartment.
Something that follows for certain from known information.
A number puzzle in which each digit appears only once in every row, column and block.

gewusst: The exercise book and pen problem is used in psychology to show how quickly our gut feeling can fool us.
The puzzle of the wolf, the goat and the cabbage is more than a thousand years old.
If 30 children all shook hands with each other, there would already be 435 handshakes.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, or the web or WWW for short, is the worldwide network of websites that you can look at with a browser. It was invented by the British researcher Tim Berners-Lee from 1989 at CERN in Geneva. Without this invention there would be no websites as we know them today.
wichtigste: Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web from 1989 at CERN in Geneva.
The web is a service on the internet, but it is not the same as the internet.
Websites are connected to each other by links.
The language HTML describes how a page is built.
You can find any page with an address, the URL.
In 1993 CERN released the web free of charge for everyone.
The world's first website ran at CERN.

abschnitte.text: The World Wide Web consists of billions of pages with text, pictures and videos. They are connected by **links**, which you can click on to jump to the next page. To look at pages, you need a **browser**. The **internet**, on the other hand, is the network of cables and computers on which the web runs. Emails also use the internet but are not part of the web.

At **CERN**, the particle physics research centre near Geneva, researchers from many countries work together. In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee proposed linking information with links so that everyone could find it easily. Together with the Belgian Robert Cailliau he developed the idea further. In 1990 the first web server ran on his computer, and in 1991 the web could also be reached outside CERN.

Every page has its own address, the **URL**, for example an address beginning with https. The browser sends a request over the internet to a server where the page is stored. The rules for this transfer are called **HTTP**. The page itself is written in the language **HTML**. The browser reads this code and uses it to display the finished page.

On 30 April 1993 CERN released the web technology so that everyone could use it free of charge. Berners-Lee had deliberately not taken out a patent. After that the web spread at breakneck speed. In 1994 he founded the W3C, an organisation that still sets rules for the web today.

Today billions of people use the web for learning, shopping, playing and staying in touch with others. **Search engines** help you find the right pages among the huge number. It is important not to believe everything on the web and to check sources. You should also protect personal data such as your address or passwords carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: A program with which you can look at websites.
A clickable reference that takes you to another page.
The language in which websites are written.
A computer that stores websites and sends them out on request.

gewusst: You can still look at the world's first website today at the address info.cern.ch.
A note was stuck on the first web server asking people not to switch the computer off.
Tim Berners-Lee was knighted by the British Queen for his invention.

teile.einleitung: The periodic table is a large table in which all the chemical elements are arranged. The Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev presented the first such arrangement in 1869 and even used it to predict elements that nobody knew yet. Today the periodic table hangs in almost every chemistry classroom in the world.
wichtigste: The periodic table arranges all known chemical elements.
Dmitri Mendeleev presented it in 1869.
He left gaps and correctly predicted elements that were still unknown.
Today 118 elements are known.
The elements are sorted by their atomic number, that is the number of protons in the atomic nucleus.
The horizontal rows are called periods, the vertical columns groups.
Elements in the same group have similar properties.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of tiny building blocks, the **atoms**. A **chemical element** is a substance made of only one kind of atom, for example oxygen, iron or gold. The periodic table arranges all the elements in a table with 7 rows and 18 columns. Each element has a box with its symbol, such as H for hydrogen or Fe for iron. Today 118 elements are known; the heaviest is called oganesson.

In the middle of the 19th century about 60 elements were known, but there was no good way of arranging them. The Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeleev** wrote the elements down in order of their weight and noticed that their properties repeated regularly. In 1869 he published his periodic table. At almost the same time the German chemist Lothar Meyer had a similar idea. But Mendeleev was bolder, because he deliberately left gaps.

Wherever an element seemed to be missing, Mendeleev left an empty space. He even described what these unknown elements would look like and how heavy they would have to be. For example, he called one of them ‘eka-aluminium’. In 1875 **gallium** was discovered, and it matched his description almost exactly. Later scandium and **germanium** followed, which brilliantly confirmed Mendeleev's system.

Today the elements are sorted by **atomic number**, which is the number of protons in the atomic nucleus. Hydrogen has the number 1, helium the number 2, carbon the number 6. The horizontal rows are called **periods**, the vertical columns **groups**. Elements in a group behave similarly: the noble gases on the far right hardly react, while the alkali metals on the far left react violently with water. Most elements are metals; they are on the left and in the middle of the table.

With the periodic table, chemists can predict how substances will react with each other. It helps in developing new materials, medicines and batteries. At school, too, it is an important tool for understanding chemistry. New, very heavy elements are now only made artificially in laboratories and usually decay in a fraction of a second. In 2019 the **International Year of the Periodic Table** was celebrated, 150 years after Mendeleev's discovery.

begriffe.erklaerung: A basic substance made of only one single kind of atom.
A tiny building block from which all substances are made.
The number of protons in the atomic nucleus; it decides an element's place in the periodic table.
Elements such as helium and neon that hardly react with other substances.

gewusst: The element with the number 101 is called mendelevium in honour of Mendeleev.
Helium was first discovered in the light of the sun and only later found on Earth.
At room temperature only two elements are liquid: mercury and bromine.

teile.einleitung: La Tomatina is a festival in the Spanish town of Buñol near Valencia. Thousands of people pelt each other with overripe tomatoes for an hour. The festival is considered the biggest tomato fight in the world.
wichtigste: La Tomatina takes place every year on the last Wednesday in August.
It is held in the small town of Buñol in the Valencia region of Spain.
The participants throw tomatoes at each other.
The actual tomato fight lasts about an hour.
The festival has existed since 1945.
Since 2013 the number of participants has been limited and you need a ticket.
Afterwards the streets are cleaned with water hoses.

abschnitte.text: La Tomatina is a cheerful **street festival** in which a whole street turns red with tomato pulp. Lorries bring many tonnes of ripe tomatoes into the old town of Buñol. People grab them and throw them at everyone nearby. By the end, everyone is standing ankle-deep in tomato juice.

**Buñol** is a small town with about 10,000 inhabitants, around 40 kilometres west of Valencia. The festival takes place on the last Wednesday in August and is part of a whole festival week. Since 2013 only about 20,000 people have been allowed to take part; in the past there were many more. Many visitors come from abroad, including from Switzerland.

The Tomatina began in 1945 with a quarrel among young people during a parade. They grabbed tomatoes from a vegetable stall and threw them at each other. The next year they did it again, and so a **tradition** was born. After the festival had been banned at times in the 1950s, it was officially allowed in 1957 following a light-hearted protest.

So that nobody gets hurt, you have to squash the tomatoes before throwing them. Bottles and other hard objects are forbidden, and you must not tear other people's T-shirts. The fight begins and ends with a **signal**, often a bang. Many people wear swimming goggles because the acid in the tomatoes stings the eyes.

After about an hour it is all over, and the fire brigade hoses the streets clean. The **acid** in the tomatoes even helps to clean the cobblestones. The participants wash at showers or in the nearby river. Cheap tomatoes that are not meant for sale are used for the fight.

begriffe.erklaerung: A big festival at which many people from an area celebrate together.
A custom that is passed on over many years.
A small town in Spain where La Tomatina takes place.
A substance that tastes sour and can, for example, sting the eyes.

gewusst: Before the start, some people try to climb a soaped wooden pole with a ham hanging at the top.
The tomato originally comes from South America and only reached Europe in the 16th century.
Following the example of La Tomatina, there are now similar tomato festivals in other countries.

teile.einleitung: Chinese New Year is the most important festival in China and is also called the Spring Festival. It falls on a different date every year because it follows the Moon. With fireworks, red lanterns and dragon dances, hundreds of millions of people welcome the new year.
wichtigste: Chinese New Year follows the Moon, so it falls on a different date every year.
It is always between 21 January and 20 February.
In China it is called the Spring Festival and is the most important family festival of the year.
Each year belongs to one of twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac.
The colour red stands for luck and is meant to drive away misfortune.
The celebrations last about two weeks and end with the Lantern Festival.
It is also celebrated in many other Asian countries and in Chinese communities worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The Chinese calendar is a **lunar calendar** that also takes the Sun into account. A lunar month lasts about 29 to 30 days, a little less than our months. The new year begins with the second new moon after the winter solstice. That is why its date shifts by a few weeks each year compared with our calendar.

Each year is linked to an animal of the **Chinese zodiac**. The twelve animals are the rat, ox, tiger, rabbit, dragon, snake, horse, goat, monkey, rooster, dog and pig. After twelve years the series starts again from the beginning. 2026 is a Year of the Horse, and 2027 will be the Year of the Goat.

Before the festival, families clean their homes thoroughly to sweep out the bad luck of the old year. Children are given **red envelopes** with money, called hongbao in Chinese. Strips of red paper with good wishes hang on doors. On New Year’s Eve the whole family eats together, and in northern China dumplings are part of the meal.

An old legend tells of a monster called **Nian**, which was afraid of noise, fire and the colour red. That is why fireworks and firecrackers go off at midnight. In parades, people dance through the streets in splendid dragon and lion costumes. On the 15th day of the new year, the festive season ends with the **Lantern Festival**.

abschnitte.titel: The biggest journey in the world
abschnitte.text: Because almost everyone travels to their family, the festival brings the biggest wave of travel in the world. In China this period is called **Chunyun**. Trains, buses and aeroplanes are full for weeks. Many people who work in big cities see their parents only once a year, at this festival.

In Vietnam, Korea, Singapore and Malaysia people also celebrate the new year by the lunar calendar. In cities such as London, San Francisco or Sydney there are big parades in the Chinatowns. Since 2024 the Spring Festival has been on UNESCO’s list of **intangible cultural heritage**. In Switzerland too, Chinese associations and restaurants invite people to celebrations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A calendar that follows the phases of the Moon.
The time when the Moon cannot be seen from Earth.
A red envelope with money that children are given at New Year.
The series of twelve animals after which years are named in China.

gewusst: Every year billions of journeys by train, bus, car and plane are counted in China around New Year.
According to a legend, a race across a river decided the order of the twelve animals, and the clever rat won because it rode on the ox’s back.
You are not supposed to clean on the first day of the new year, so that you do not sweep the good luck straight out again.

teile.einleitung: The Higgs boson is a tiny elementary particle that explains why other particles have mass. Its existence was already predicted in 1964. But it was only detected in 2012 at CERN near Geneva, using the world's largest particle accelerator.
wichtigste: The Higgs boson is an elementary particle.
It belongs to the Higgs field, which gives other particles their mass.
Peter Higgs and other physicists predicted it in 1964.
On 4 July 2012 CERN announced its discovery.
It was found with the Large Hadron Collider, or LHC for short.
In 2013 Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in Physics.
The particle decays again after an unimaginably short time.

abschnitte.text: Everything around us is made of tiny building blocks, the **elementary particles**. The **Higgs boson** is one of them and an important part of the so-called **Standard Model** of physics. It is closely linked to an invisible field that fills the whole universe. Without this field many particles would have no mass, and there would be no atoms, no stars and no people.

abschnitte.titel: How does the Higgs field work?
abschnitte.text: You can imagine the **Higgs field** as an invisible bath of syrup. Some particles glide through it almost unhindered, others are slowed down a lot. The more strongly a particle interacts with the field, the heavier it is. The Higgs boson is, so to speak, a small wave in this field.

In 1964 the Briton **Peter Higgs** and the Belgians François Englert and Robert Brout independently published the idea of this field. For almost 50 years researchers searched in vain for the matching particle. This needed huge energies that could only be reached with new accelerators. Peter Higgs lived to see the discovery and died in 2024.

The **Large Hadron Collider** lies about 100 metres underground on the border between Switzerland and France. In its 27-kilometre ring, protons are brought almost to the speed of light and fired at each other. The huge detectors ATLAS and CMS recorded billions of these collisions. On 4 July 2012 **CERN** announced that both experiments had found the Higgs boson.

In 2013 Higgs and Englert received the **Nobel Prize** in Physics; Brout had already died. The Higgs boson is about 130 times as heavy as a proton. Researchers at CERN are still studying its properties very closely. They hope to find clues to new physics, for example about mysterious dark matter.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle that is not made up of even smaller parts.
Tells you how heavy something is and how strongly it resists movement.
A facility that makes tiny particles extremely fast and lets them collide.
The European Organization for Nuclear Research near Geneva, one of the largest research centres in the world.

gewusst: Newspapers often called the Higgs boson the ‘God particle’, which many physicists did not like at all.
CERN was founded in 1954, and the World Wide Web was also invented at CERN in 1989.
The Italian Fabiola Gianotti presented the ATLAS results in 2012 and later became Director-General of CERN.

tzum7ig.t: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen

teile.einleitung: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is a famous document from the French Revolution. The French National Assembly adopted it in August 1789. It states that all people are born free and equal in rights.
wichtigste: The Declaration was adopted by the French National Assembly on 26 August 1789.
It was written shortly after the start of the French Revolution.
Its first article says that people are born free and equal in rights.
It has 17 articles.
Among other things, it protects freedom of opinion and property.
At first it did not apply to women and slaves.
It influenced many later constitutions, including that of Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen is a short text with 17 articles. It describes rights that belong to every person simply because they are a human being. Such rights are called **human rights**. It also names rights that you have as a citizen of a state, the **civil rights**.

In the summer of 1789 France was in turmoil, and on 14 July the people of Paris stormed the **Bastille** prison. The newly formed **National Assembly** wanted to abolish the old privileges of king, nobility and Church. On 26 August 1789 it adopted the Declaration. One of the authors of the draft was the Marquis de La Fayette.

The ideas came from the **Enlightenment**, a movement of thinkers such as Montesquieu, Voltaire and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who came from Geneva. They demanded that people should think for themselves and live freely. Another model was the United States Declaration of Independence of 1776. Before that, the king in France had almost unlimited power.

The Declaration says that all people are equal before the law. Nobody may be arrested or punished except according to the law. Everyone may freely say and write what they think, as long as they respect the laws. Power in the state should come from the **people** and be divided between different branches.

At that time “man” mainly meant men. That is why the writer **Olympe de Gouges** wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen in 1791. In the French colonies slavery was only abolished in 1794 and was later brought back. It took a long time before the rights really applied to everyone.

The Declaration is still part of the French constitution today. It was a model for many constitutions in Europe and around the world, including the Swiss Federal Constitution. In 1948 the United Nations adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**, which takes up many of its ideas. In Switzerland, fundamental rights are now set out in the Federal Constitution.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that belong to every person, wherever they live.
An elected assembly that makes laws for the whole nation.
A period in the 18th century in which reason and freedom were especially stressed.
The most important law of a state, which lays down the basic rules.

gewusst: Olympe de Gouges, who demanded equal rights for women, was executed in 1793 during the Revolution.
The Declaration begins with an introduction saying that forgetting human rights is the cause of the misfortunes of nations.
14 July, the day of the storming of the Bastille, is today France’s national holiday.
